title: Palatal Island Flap With Adjuvant Radiotherapy for Hard Palate Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma: 2-year Outcomes.
abstract: Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) of the minor salivary glands most commonly arises in the hard palate and exhibits perineural invasion, indolent growth, and late recurrence, often requiring multimodal therapy. Reconstruction must restore oronasal separation, speech, and deglutition; data regarding the tolerance of palatal island flaps to postoperative radiotherapy and long-term functional outcomes remain limited. A 35-year-old woman with T1N0M0 ACC of the right hard palate (American Joint Committee on Cancer, 8th edition) underwent wide local excision with partial palatal ostectomy followed by reconstruction using a contralateral palatal island flap. After complete mucosal healing, adjuvant intensity-modulated radiotherapy (66 Gy in 33 fractions) was administered. Two-year outcomes were assessed using Thai-language validated versions of the EORTC QLQ-C30, EORTC QLQ-HN43, FACT-H&N, and UW-QOL questionnaires. Final pathology demonstrated cribriform and tubular ACC with perineural invasion. The tumor approached the medial (0.4 mm) and lateral (1.7 mm) margins, which were close but uninvolved. Acute toxicity consisted of grade 2 donor-site oral mucositis treated with topical triamcinolone. At 2-year follow-up, surveillance with magnetic resonance imaging of the skull base, computed tomography of the chest, and bone scintigraphy demonstrated no evidence of locoregional recurrence or distant metastasis. Speech was fully intelligible on speech-language pathology assessment, the Functional Oral Intake Scale score was 7, and quality-of-life outcomes remained favorable across all instruments. This case suggested that a palatal island flap may tolerate adjuvant radiotherapy when irradiation is delivered after complete flap healing, with favorable oncological, functional, and quality-of-life outcomes at 2 years.

A 35-year-old woman with T1N0M0 ACC of the right hard palate (American Joint Committee on Cancer, 8th edition) underwent wide local excision with partial palatal ostectomy followed by reconstruction using a contralateral palatal island flap. After complete mucosal healing, adjuvant intensity-modulated radiotherapy (66 Gy in 33 fractions) was administered. Two-year outcomes were assessed using Thai-language validated versions of the EORTC QLQ-C30, EORTC QLQ-HN43, FACT-H&N, and UW-QOL questionnaires. Final pathology demonstrated cribriform and tubular ACC with perineural invasion. The tumor approached the medial (0.4 mm) and lateral (1.7 mm) margins, which were close but uninvolved. Acute toxicity consisted of grade 2 donor-site oral mucositis treated with topical triamcinolone. At 2-year follow-up, surveillance with magnetic resonance imaging of the skull base, computed tomography of the chest, and bone scintigraphy demonstrated no evidence of locoregional recurrence or distant metastasis. title: Biopsy of Secondary Angiosarcoma Arising in Native Mastectomy Skin of a Reconstructed Breast Without Prior Radiotherapy.
abstract: Secondary breast angiosarcoma usually develops after radiotherapy or in the setting of chronic lymphedema. We report a rare case of non-radiation-associated secondary cutaneous angiosarcoma arising in the native mastectomy skin overlying a reconstructed breast after immediate tissue expander placement and delayed deep inferior epigastric perforator flap reconstruction for breast cancer. The patient's clinical course, imaging, histopathological findings, and treatment were retrospectively reviewed. The clinicopathological features were compared with previously reported cases of angiosarcoma arising after breast reconstruction without radiotherapy before angiosarcoma onset. A 45-year-old woman underwent right mastectomy, axillary dissection, and immediate tissue expander placement for right breast cancer (T2N1M0, stage IIB), followed by delayed deep inferior epigastric perforator flap reconstruction 1 year later. No adjuvant radiotherapy was administered. Three years after the initial breast cancer surgery, progressive purpura and dark violaceous nodules developed in the native mastectomy skin. Skin biopsy confirmed cutaneous angiosarcoma. Histology showed atypical endothelial proliferation forming irregular vascular channels; tumor cells were positive for ETS-related gene and cluster of differentiation 34; the molecular immunology borstel-1 index was approximately 40%; and MYC proto-oncogene expression was observed in 60%-70% of tumor cells. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography showed no distant metastasis. Because the cutaneous disease was diffuse and surgical local control was judged difficult, multimodal treatment with pazopanib and radiotherapy (70 Gy) was initiated, followed by trastuzumab plus paclitaxel for local progression. No distant metastasis was present at the latest follow-up, although local control remained challenging. Persistent or progressive dermatitis-like lesions in postmastectomy breast skin should prompt early biopsy even in patients without prior radiotherapy.

title: Congenital Melanocytic Nevus Mimicking a Coccygeal Pad in the Sacrococcygeal Region.
abstract: Congenital melanocytic nevus (CMN) is a benign melanocytic proliferative lesion that presents at birth or in early infancy. When the lesion extends into the deep dermis or subcutaneous tissue, it can form a mass that is clinically and radiologically indistinguishable from other soft tissue tumors. We report a case of sacrococcygeal CMN mimicking a coccygeal pad. An 18-year-old man presented with a sacrococcygeal mass and tenderness. Magnetic resonance imaging and needle biopsy findings suggested a coccygeal pad. Because of persistent pain and the patient's desire for removal, the mass was excised under general anesthesia with periosteal inclusion, and the resulting 95 × 50 mm defect was reconstructed using a right superior gluteal artery perforator flap. Histopathological examination confirmed CMN without malignant features. The flap survived completely, and the postoperative course was uneventful. Tenderness resolved completely, and no local or symptomatic recurrence was observed at 6 months. CMN should be considered in the differential diagnosis of sacrococcygeal masses, and needle biopsy may be insufficient for diagnosing deeply infiltrating lesions.

title: The Hidden Trap: Tolosa-Hunt Syndrome Masking Entrapped Great Occipital Nerve-A Case of Headache Surgery.
abstract: Headache syndromes may coexist with peripheral nerve entrapment, which can obscure the true pain generator and delay effective treatment. Tolosa-Hunt syndrome is a rare, painful ophthalmoplegia syndrome characterized by unilateral orbital pain and cranial nerve palsy, often showing a marked response to corticosteroids. We report the case of a 56-year-old woman with a long history of migraine who developed recurrent right-sided orbital pain, maxillary pain, and ophthalmoplegia. She was diagnosed with Tolosa-Hunt syndrome by an experienced neurologist after skull magnetic resonance imaging and clinical evaluation. Because steroids and anti-inflammatory treatment produced only partial relief, and because she also had occipital pain with a positive Tinel sign over the greater occipital nerve, occipital neuralgia was suspected. A diagnostic block of the right greater occipital nerve provided partial improvement, after which right-sided surgical decompression of the nerve was performed. At 1-year follow-up, the patient had no residual surgical sensory deficit, no recurrent severe orbital or maxillary pain, and a marked reduction in attack frequency and intensity. Her Migraine Disability Assessment score improved from 18 to 4, and medication use decreased to sporadic use of simple analgesics and triptans. In selected patients, rare headache syndromes may coexist with occult peripheral nerve entrapment. Persistent symptoms despite appropriate medical treatment should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis and targeted evaluation for occipital neuralgia.

title: Impact of body composition on clinical outcomes in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background Abnormalities in body composition are common in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC); however, their impact across different treatment modalities remains poorly understood. We systematically reviewed the prognostic value of body composition in patients with HCC, stratified by curative, locoregional, and systemic therapies. Methods Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science (January 2015-March 2025) for studies reporting associations between CT/MRI or bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA)-assessed body composition and outcomes in HCC. Results Ninety-two studies were included (35 curative, 10 locoregional, 39 systemic, 8 mixed). Sarcopenia prevalence ranged from 6.4% to 62.8% (median study-level prevalence 38%-50% depending on treatment stratum). Sarcopenia independently predicted worse overall survival across all strata: curative (HR 1.52-3.76), locoregional (HR 1.72-2.51), and systemic therapies (HR 1.34-2.20). Sarcopenic obesity conferred the highest risk in the curative setting (HR up to 3.15). In systemic therapy, myosteatosis independently predicted mortality (HR 1.45-2.01), whereas visceral adiposity was protective (HR 0.56-0.66). In a random-effects meta-analysis of 44 studies, sarcopenia was associated with a pooled HR of 1.85 (95% CI 1.75-1.94; I2=0%), with consistent effects across curative (HR 1.86), locoregional (HR 2.10), and systemic strata (HR 1.71). Sarcopenia also predicted recurrence after curative treatment (pooled HR 1.71, 95% CI 1.61-1.82; k=14). Conclusions Sarcopenia predicts mortality in HCC, independently of treatment modality. Visceral adiposity appears detrimental after curative treatment but may be paradoxically protective during systemic therapy. Body composition should be integrated into clinical decision-making in HCC, though a clear consensus on measurement standardization is needed.

title: AASLD EXPO: Liver biopsy.
abstract: Background Liver biopsy is a foundational tool in hepatology, providing direct histologic assessment of hepatic parenchyma. Although noninvasive approaches have substantially reduced the need for biopsy in practice, it continues to play a critical role in diagnosis, staging, and therapeutic decision-making across a broad spectrum of liver disorders. Methods This Expert Practice Opinion (EXPO) document was created by a writing group of subject matter experts appointed by the AASLD Practice Guidelines Committee. Writing group members performed a targeted literature review and created expert opinion statements that were unanimously agreed upon. Results Histopathologic evaluation of the liver is utilized for 3 major indications: (1) to establish a diagnosis, (2) to stage the severity of inflammation and/or fibrosis, and (3) to enhance clinical management of liver disease. Liver biopsy can be performed using a percutaneous, transjugular, or endoscopic ultrasound approach. Percutaneous liver biopsy is used in most patients, though transjugular liver biopsy is often performed in those with ascites or coagulopathy and/or when hepatic venous pressure gradient measurement is desired. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided liver biopsy is particularly attractive when endoscopy to evaluate and treat varices or portal pressure gradient measurement is desired. The different biopsy techniques appear to have similar safety profiles and yield adequate tissue when performed by experts. Liver biopsy has limitations, including sampling variability, interobserver differences in interpretation, and procedural complications. Conclusions Liver biopsy continues to play an essential role in contemporary hepatology practice. Recent advances include the introduction of endoscopic ultrasound liver biopsy. Evolving applications-including the potential for molecular profiling, use of digital pathology, and assessment of therapeutic response-underscore the continued relevance of tissue-based evaluation in precision hepatology.

title: Baveno VI criteria validation and development of a new non-invasive strategy for varices rule-out in patients with HCC (SAPHE-R: Stiffness, ALBI, Platelets, HEpatocellular carcinoma Rule).
abstract: Accuracy of Baveno criteria for avoiding endoscopy in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is uncertain, and systematic upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (UGE) may not be necessary. We evaluated Baveno VI criteria performance in this population and developed an alternative non-invasive rule to exclude esophagogastric varices of any grade, rather than high-risk varices (HRV). Patients with BCLC 0-C HCC and compensated advanced chronic liver disease (cACLD) from Italian Liver Cancer (ITA.LI.CA) database, with available liver stiffness measurement (LSM), UGE, and blood tests within six months of diagnosis, were included. Independent predictors of varices identified by logistic regression were combined through grid-search to derive a rule-out strategy (SAPHE-R), validated by bootstrap-resampling and in an independent cohort (Vienna). The derivation cohort comprised 598 patients (age, 69 years; male sex, 75.3%; viral etiology, 69.3%; BCLC 0/A, 77.9%; ALBI 1, 54.2%; varices, 33.4%; HRV, 11.2%). Baveno VI criteria missed 8.5% of varices and 6.0% of HRV, sparing 31.1% of UGE. Independent predictors of varices were incorporated into SAPHE-R (LSM≤16 kPa, platelet count ≥160×10⁹/L, ALBI grade 1), which missed 4.0% of varices (HRV 3.0%, spared UGE 17.6%). In the validation cohort (n=149), SAPHE-R missed 4.8% of varices (HRV 3.1%, spared UGE 14.8%). Results remained consistent in sensitivity analyses. In an exploratory analysis, no HVPG-defined CSPH was observed among SAPHE-R rule-out patients (0/22). Baveno VI criteria showed suboptimal performance in patients with HCC and cACLD, whereas SAPHE-R provided a reliable non-invasive strategy to rule out varices, facilitating variceal risk assessment in patients with HCC.

title: TRACTION-INDUCED STRUCTURAL FAILURE STATES IN MACULAR HOLE FORMATION REVEALED BY VOLUME-RENDERED SWEPT SOURCE OCT.
abstract: Purpose To analyze macular hole development using three-dimensional visualization of vitreomacular architecture volume-rendered optical coherence tomography (OCT) and to interpret observed anatomical configurations using structural and mechanical principles. Methods This retrospective observational study included eyes with developing macular holes imaged using a swept source OCT. Volumetric data sets of the macula and overlying vitreous were processed with extended dynamic-range processing and rendered to permit three-dimensional visualization of vitreous attachment, deformation, and retinal structural changes. Anatomical configurations were evaluated descriptively. Terminology was applied to denote OCT-based structural failure states without implying a fixed temporal sequence. Results Seventeen eyes of 13 patients were analyzed. Persistent vitreous attachment to the central macula was associated with a range of distinct anatomical configurations, including inner macular cavitation, combined inner cavitation with outer retinal separation, outer macular holes with preserved inner retina, inner lamellar holes, and full-thickness macular holes. Volume rendering demonstrated asymmetric vitreous attachment, catenary-like vitreous geometry, tears in the posterior cortical vitreous, vitreous prolapse, and frequent retinal flaps that were not readily apparent on conventional planar imaging. Longitudinal imaging showed variable transitions between structural configurations associated with changes in vitreous attachment rather than a uniform progression through predefined stages. Conclusion Volume-rendered swept source OCT enables direct visualization of vitreomacular architecture during macular hole development. The observed anatomical configurations are best understood as traction-induced structural failure states of the central macula rather than as a linear temporal staging sequence. This framework better accounts for the diversity, asymmetry, and nonuniform evolution of macular hole morphology observed in vivo.

title: Macular Laceration Following Intravitreal Injection in a Nanophthalmic Eye: Management with Pars Plana Vitrectomy.
abstract: Purpose To report a case of macular laceration following intravitreal injection in a nanophthalmic eye and its surgical management. Methods A nanophthalmic patient presented with visual decline after intravitreal bevacizumab injection. Multimodal imaging demonstrated a full-thickness macular defect, vitreous hemorrhage, and epiretinal membrane (ERM), consistent with suspected needle-induced injury. Following failed medical therapy, 27-gauge pars plana vitrectomy with internal limiting membrane peeling and gas tamponade was performed using modified sclerotomy placement. Results Surgery was successfully completed with treatment of an intraoperative peripheral retinal break. At 3.5 months, visual acuity improved from hand movements to 20/80. Optical coherence tomography confirmed ERM resolution, retinal reattachment, and restoration of macular architecture without cystoid macular edema or uveal effusion. Conclusion Macular laceration is a rare but potentially vision-threatening complication of intravitreal injection, with increased risk in anatomically crowded eyes such as nanophthalmos. Careful surgical planning allows successful vitrectomy with favorable anatomical and visual outcomes in this high-risk population.

title: Presumed Primary CD79B+ Vitreoretinal Lymphoma Mimicking an Ischemia-Like Macular Lesion.
abstract: Purpose To report a case of presumed primary vitreoretinal lymphoma (PVRL) mimicking an ischemia-like macular lesion. Methods Single-patient case report. Results A 74-year-old male patient presented with sudden vision loss up to the hand-motion level in his right eye. Fundus examination revealed a creamy, white-colored, ischemic-appearing macular area excluding the foveal region. Numerous vitreous cells and snowball-like opacities were observed. No relative afferent pupillary defect was evident, and no intraorbital mass or signs of active inflammation were revealed by contrast-enhanced cranial magnetic resonance imaging. Fluorescence angiography revealed a late-phase leopard-spot pattern of hyperfluorescence, whereas optical coherence tomography showed banded subretinal exudates with hyperreflective, vitelliform lesions within the retinal pigment epithelium. Cytological examination of the vitreous was negative for malignant cells. Using next-generation sequencing, the multigene mutation analysis revealed pathogenic CD79B, BTG2, and PIM1 mutations, supporting the diagnosis of PVRL. Twenty-two months later, in response to visual acuity (best-corrected) reduction from 0.5 LogMAR (20/63) at baseline to hand motions, intravitreal methotrexate therapy was initiated in the left eye, which decreased the vitreous cell density. The right eye has since remained stable at 0.2 LogMAR (20/32). Conclusion Presumed PVRL can mimic ischemic-appearing macular lesions and should be considered in the differential diagnosis of atypical ischemic retinal lesions. A thorough diagnostic workup should include multimodal imaging and cranial magnetic resonance imaging. When cytology is inconclusive, molecular genetic testing via NGS becomes a crucial tool, particularly when clinical suspicion remains high.

title: Retinoschisis-Associated Retinal Detachment in Choroideremia: A Surgical Conundrum.
abstract: Purpose To describe a case of retinoschisis-associated retinal detachment (RD) in a patient with genetically confirmed choroideremia and discuss implications for surveillance and surgical management. Methods A case report of a 43-year-old man with genotypically confirmed choroideremia, CHM c.242_245 deletion, who developed rhegmatogenous RD following progression of peripheral retinoschisis. Multimodal imaging, including optical coherence tomography (OCT), B-scan ultrasonography, ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM), and fundus autofluorescence (AF) were utilized for diagnosis and surgical planning. Results The patient presented with acute visual decline from 20/20 Snellen to 20/100 Snellen in the affected eye following progression of temporal retinoschisis into the fovea. OCT demonstrated schisis cavities with subretinal fluid extending to the fovea. B-scan demonstrated shallow temporal subretinal fluid involving the macula, and UBM was suggestive of multiple small anterior holes within the retinoschisis, though these were not clearly identified on examination with indirect fundoscopy. Surgical repair with a high posterior encircling scleral buckle (#277 tire) with cryopexy achieved foveal reattachment, schisis cavity collapse, and visual recovery to 20/25 Snellen. Conclusions This case represents the first documented retinoschisis-associated RD in choroideremia. Progressive degeneration of the RPE, choroid, and retinal layers may create structural instability predisposing to RD when retinoschisis progresses. This mechanism should theoretically make surgical reattachment challenging. This case highlights the need for risk stratification, close follow-up, and early surgical intervention to prevent reversible vision loss in patients with retinoschisis, RD, and choroideremia.

title: Paracentral Acute Middle Maculopathy Prompting Diagnosis of Severe Aortic Regurgitation and Ascending Aortic Aneurysm.
abstract: Purpose To report a case of paracentral acute middle maculopathy (PAMM) in which persistent paracentral dysfunction prompted cardiovascular investigation and diagnosis of severe aortic regurgitation, reduced ejection fraction, and ascending aortic aneurysm. Methods Longitudinal ophthalmic assessment, multimodal retinal imaging, Humphrey SITA Central 10-2 testing, cardiovascular evaluation, surgical findings, histopathology, and targeted aortopathy genetic testing were reviewed. Results A 44-year-old man presented with intermittent right-eye visual disturbance and persistent paracentral scotoma after non-explanatory neuroimaging. Unaided visual acuity remained 20/25 (6/7.5; approximately 0.10 logMAR) in each eye, intraocular pressure was 16-19 mmHg, and anterior-segment examination was unremarkable. Multimodal imaging supported PAMM, with structural OCT inner retinal/inner nuclear layer involvement and qualitative OCT-A/fluorescein angiographic parafoveal perfusion compromise. The affected inner retinal/inner nuclear layer region decreased from 45 micrometres to 32 micrometres. Right-eye Humphrey SITA Central 10-2 mean deviation worsened from -3.67 dB on 03 March 2020 to -5.19 dB in February 2026 despite unchanged central acuity. Cardiovascular assessment revealed a 5.5-cm ascending aortic aneurysm, severe aortic regurgitation, and left-ventricular ejection fraction of 49%. The patient underwent elective Bentall procedure, with postoperative ejection-fraction improvement to 55%. No postoperative quantitative OCT-A reperfusion claim is made. Conclusion PAMM may warrant systemic cardiovascular assessment when ocular findings do not fully explain persistent paracentral dysfunction. This case supports cautious multidisciplinary evaluation while avoiding unsupported claims of causality, quantitative OCT-A perfusion deficit, or postoperative retinal reperfusion.

title: Retinal manifestations of neglected tropical diseases.
abstract: Purpose of review Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) are increasingly encountered outside endemic regions due to global migration, international travel, and climate change. This review addresses the timely need for ophthalmologists to recognize the retinal manifestations of NTDs, as these conditions now appear in developed nations where clinicians may have limited prior exposure. Recent findings Modern multimodal imaging has revealed distinct retinal patterns that are frequently seen in NTDs. Dengue and chikungunya present with maculopathy, foveolitis, and retinal hemorrhages. Onchocerciasis causes progressive chorioretinal atrophy and optic nerve involvement leading to vision loss. Neurocysticercosis manifests as subretinal or intravitreal cysts with visible scolices. Schistosomiasis produces chorioretinal granulomas and neuroretinitis. Leishmaniasis presents with posterior uveitis and chorioretinal lesions. African trypanosomiasis demonstrates choroidal infiltrates and retinal vasculitis. Chagas disease shows microvasculopathy with retinal hemorrhages, while leprosy causes chronic uveitis with iris pearls and chorioretinal scarring. Summary Recognition of retinal manifestations is crucial for NTD diagnosis and management. Ophthalmologists must maintain high clinical suspicion based on travel history and systemic symptoms. Collaborative care with infectious disease specialists and utilization of appropriate diagnostic modalities facilitate optimal outcomes and prevent vision loss while addressing broader public health implications.

African trypanosomiasis demonstrates choroidal infiltrates and retinal vasculitis. Chagas disease shows microvasculopathy with retinal hemorrhages, while leprosy causes chronic uveitis with iris pearls and chorioretinal scarring.

Summary

Recognition of retinal manifestations is crucial for NTD diagnosis and management. Ophthalmologists must maintain high clinical suspicion based on travel history and systemic symptoms. Collaborative care with infectious disease specialists and utilization of appropriate diagnostic modalities facilitate optimal outcomes and prevent vision loss while addressing broader public health implications.

title: Anterior Segment Ischemia and Neurotrophic Keratopathy Following Ultrasound Cycloplasty in Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma.
abstract: Ultrasound cycloplasty (UCP) is a minimally invasive, non-incisional glaucoma procedure that has emerged in recent years and is generally associated with few complications. We report a case of a patient with acute angle-closure glaucoma underwent UCP for IOP control. She developed iris neovascularization and neurotrophic keratopathy（NK）at postoperative week 6, followed by hypopyon, flattening of the anterior chamber, and thinning of the peripheral cornea at postoperative week 11, 12, and 14, respectively. We concluded that UCP can lead to anterior segment ischemia (ASI) and NK, which manifest as iris neovascularization, painless corneal epithelial defects, peripheral corneal thinning, hypopyon, and flattening of the anterior chamber. Preoperative screening for high-risk factors is essential before performing UCP.

title: Chorioretinal Scars in Congenital Cytomegalovirus Infection Following Prenatal Valacyclovir Therapy.
abstract: Background Congenital cytomegalovirus infection is the most common congenital infection. Ocular abnormalities affect approximately 14% of symptomatic children, but fewer than 1% of asymptomatic children. Prenatal valacyclovir reduces vertical transmission, but ophthalmic outcomes in exposed infants are poorly described. Methods We describe 2 neonates with congenital cytomegalovirus confirmed by amniotic fluid and urine polymerase chain reaction following first-trimester maternal primary infection. Both mothers received high-dose valacyclovir (8 g daily) from 13 weeks' gestation. Infants underwent neonatal evaluation, including dilated fundus examination and multimodal retinal imaging. Results Maternal treatment continued to 36 weeks in 1 pregnancy and was discontinued at 22 weeks in the other, after amniocentesis. Both infants had macular chorioretinal scarring. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated focal ellipsoid zone disruption in a clinically normal fellow eye in 1 infant. Cranial ultrasonography demonstrated caudothalamic and temporal lobe cysts with lenticulostriate vasculopathy in 1 infant and isolated lenticulostriate vasculopathy in the other. Physical and neurologic examinations, head circumference, full blood count, liver function and auditory brainstem responses were normal in both. Both were classified as symptomatic with central nervous system involvement on the basis of ocular findings and therefore received valganciclovir for a planned 6 months. Retinal findings were stable at 3 months. Conclusions Macular chorioretinal scarring was present in both infants despite otherwise limited clinical findings, and the extent of cranial imaging abnormality did not correspond to ocular involvement. Ophthalmologic examination determined disease classification and management. These observations do not permit conclusions regarding the effect of prenatal valacyclovir on ocular outcome.

title: Group A Streptococcus in an Unexpected Site: Temporal Pyomyositis in 2 Children.
abstract: Background Pyomyositis is an uncommon bacterial infection of skeletal muscle. Group A Streptococcus (GAS) accounts for a smaller proportion of pediatric cases, and temporal muscle involvement is exceptionally rare. Case description We report 2 previously healthy children, a 7-year-old boy and a 6-year-old girl, who presented with acute otitis media (AOM) and painful unilateral temporomandibular swelling. Computed tomography revealed AOM with temporal myositis, complicated by mastoiditis in the first case. Both were treated with intravenous antibiotics, and the first case required drainage and mastoidectomy, with full recovery. GAS was isolated in both cases. Conclusions GAS temporal pyomyositis should be considered in children presenting with AOM and painful temporal swelling. Imaging is crucial for diagnosis and assessment of disease extent. Surgical management should be individualized.

title: Parasitic Infections of the Lacrimal System: A Major Review of Etiology, Clinical Presentation, and Management.
abstract: Purpose Parasitic infections of the lacrimal system are rare and often under-recognized causes of lacrimal pathology. Their clinical presentation frequently mimics more common conditions such as chronic dacryocystitis, leading to diagnostic challenges and delays in appropriate management. This study aims to systematically review the literature on parasitic infections of the lacrimal system and to characterize their etiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic approaches, management strategies, and outcomes. Methods A systematic review was conducted across MEDLINE, Embase, Emcare, and PubMed from inception to March 2026. Studies reporting parasitic infections involving the lacrimal apparatus were included. Data on demographics, clinical presentation, anatomical involvement, causative organisms, diagnostic methods, treatment, and outcomes were extracted. Due to heterogeneity and predominance of case reports and small series, a qualitative descriptive analysis was performed. Results A total of 44 studies comprising 172 cases were included. Rhinosporidium seeberi was the most frequently reported pathogen, accounting for 147 cases (85.5%), followed by Leishmania (8 cases, 4.7%) and Ascaris lumbricoides (7 cases, 4.1%). The lacrimal sac was the most commonly involved site. Clinical presentation was nonspecific, with epiphora and medial canthal swelling predominating. Diagnosis was most often established by histopathology following surgical intervention. Management varied by etiology, with surgical excision commonly used for rhinosporidiosis and mechanical extraction for helminthic infections. Outcomes were generally favorable, although recurrence was reported, particularly in R. seeberi infections. Conclusions Parasitic infections of the lacrimal system are rare but clinically important, with diverse presentations and management approaches. Increased awareness is essential for early diagnosis and appropriate treatment. Further studies with standardized reporting are needed to optimize management strategies.

title: Impact of different intraocular pressures during cataract surgery on retinal perfusion in eyes with diabetic retinopathy: randomized clinical trial.
abstract: Purpose To study the effect of varying preset intraocular pressure (IOP) levels during phacoemulsification on the retinal perfusion using optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) in eyes with nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR). Setting Iladevi Cataract & IOL Research Centre, Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India. Design Randomized clinical trial. Methods Patients undergoing cataract surgery with NPDR were randomized (1:1) to low (20 mm Hg) and high (55 mm Hg) intraoperative IOP. Primary outcome measure was percentage (%) change in central retinal vessel density (CRVD) on OCTA. Secondary outcome measures included impact on optic nerve perfusion (Flux Index [FI]) on OCTA and comparison of postoperative IOP. Outcome measures were evaluated within 2 hours of surgery, as well as on days 1, 7, and 30 postoperatively. Results 40 eyes (40 patients) were recruited in each group. CRVD increased postoperatively, with a statistically significant increase at 1 week and 1 month in the low (vs high) IOP group. The reduction in perfusion density in the radial peripapillary capillary region did not differ significantly between groups. FI improved postoperatively in both groups, with significant improvement in the low (vs high) IOP group at each follow-up visit. Postoperative IOP was comparable between groups, with a trend toward higher levels in the high IOP group. Conclusions Low IOP (20 mm Hg) during cataract surgery of eyes with preexisting vascular compromise may have a beneficial effect on macular and optic nerve head perfusion, especially in the early postoperative period.

title: Diagnostic Value of Prostate-specific Membrane Antigen Positron Emission Tomography / Magnetic Resonance Imaging in Selected Men with Equivocal Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System Category 3 Lesion (PANDORA): A Prospective Paired Diagnostic Study.
abstract: Purpose Equivocal Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) category 3 lesions carry an intermediate risk of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa). We evaluated the diagnostic value of prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography/magnetic resonance imaging (PSMA PET/MRI) with [18F]JK-PSMA-7, performed after diagnostic MRI, in biopsy-eligible men with an equivocal PI-RADS category 3 lesion. We hypothesized that PSMA PET-targeted biopsy would detect more csPCa than MRI-targeted biopsy. Materials and methods We conducted a single-center prospective paired diagnostic study from November 2023 to February 2026. Biopsy-eligible men with an equivocal PI-RADS category 3 lesion on diagnostic MRI and ≥1 high-risk feature underwent pre-biopsy PSMA PET/MRI, with positivity defined as a PRIMARY score ≥3, followed by transperineal MRI-targeted, PSMA PET-targeted when positive, and systematic biopsy. The primary outcome was the per-patient csPCa detection rate (International Society of Urological Pathology grade group ≥2 with ≥10% Gleason pattern 4) of PSMA PET-targeted vs MRI-targeted biopsy, assessed with the exact McNemar test. Results Of 83 men assessed, 66 completed PSMA PET/MRI and biopsy. PSMA PET was positive in 21 of 66 (32%). PSMA PET-targeted biopsy detected csPCa in 10 of 66 (15%) vs 4 of 66 (6%) for MRI-targeted biopsy (difference 9%; 95% CI 2%-18%; P = .03). Sensitivity, specificity, and negative predictive value of PSMA PET were 100%, 82%, and 100%. Biopsy would have been avoided in 45 of 66 men (68%) with a negative result, none of whom had csPCa. Conclusions In biopsy-eligible men with an equivocal PI-RADS category 3 lesion, PSMA PET-targeted biopsy detected more csPCa than MRI-targeted biopsy. The high negative predictive value suggests that deferral of biopsy after a negative result merits evaluation in larger multicentre studies.

title: Diagnostic Strategies After Negative Colposcopy in High-Grade Cervical Cytology: A Multicenter Randomized Trial.
abstract: Objectives To compare diagnostic strategies for detecting HSIL or worse (HSIL+) in women with high-grade cytology and negative colposcopy, and to assess whether sequential HPV testing, liquid-based cytology (LBC), and endocervical sampling improve diagnostic safety. Methods This is a multicenter randomized clinical trial conducted at 4 referral centers between 2021 and 2022. Women with ASC-H or worse cytology and negative colposcopy underwent HPV testing and LBC. Participants were randomized to endocervical brushing (EB) or endocervical curettage (ECC). The reference standard was histopathology from excisional procedures or structured follow-up. Diagnostic performance (sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and accuracy) was calculated for individual tests and predefined combinations (AND ALL and MAJORITY rules). Absolute differences between strategies were analyzed. Invalid results were classified as failures (false negatives or false positives) according to the final diagnosis. Results Among 257 women, 35 cases of HSIL+ were identified. HPV testing showed the highest sensitivity (94.3%) and negative predictive value (98.6%), whereas LBC demonstrated higher specificity (84.9%) and accuracy (84.1%). The combination of HPV and LBC (AND rule) improved specificity to 91.7% with a sensitivity of 77.1%. Adding EB (MAJORITY rule) increased sensitivity to 100% (absolute increase 22.9%) but reduced specificity to 82.3%. ECC showed lower sensitivity (61.1%) and higher inadequacy rates (21.3%). Conclusions In women with high-grade cytology and negative colposcopy, HPV testing followed by LBC provides a balanced diagnostic strategy. To compare diagnostic strategies for detecting HSIL or worse (HSIL+) in women with high-grade cytology and negative colposcopy, and to assess whether sequential HPV testing, liquid-based cytology (LBC), and endocervical sampling improve diagnostic safety.

This is a multicenter randomized clinical trial conducted at 4 referral centers between 2021 and 2022. Women with ASC-H or worse cytology and negative colposcopy underwent HPV testing and LBC. Participants were randomized to endocervical brushing (EB) or endocervical curettage (ECC). The reference standard was histopathology from excisional procedures or structured follow-up. Diagnostic performance (sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and accuracy) was calculated for individual tests and predefined combinations (AND ALL and MAJORITY rules). Absolute differences between strategies were analyzed. Invalid results were classified as failures (false negatives or false positives) according to the final diagnosis.

Results

Among 257 women, 35 cases of HSIL+ were identified. HPV testing showed the highest sensitivity (94.3%) and negative predictive value (98.6%), whereas LBC demonstrated higher specificity (84.9%) and accuracy (84.1%). The combination of HPV and LBC (AND rule) improved specificity to 91.7% with a sensitivity of 77.1%. Conclusions

In women with high-grade cytology and negative colposcopy, HPV testing followed by LBC provides a balanced diagnostic strategy. The addition of endocervical brushing may increase sensitivity in selected high-risk cases and improve the detection of HSIL+ after negative colposcopy.

title: Optimizing Cochlear Implant Outcomes in Cochlear Nerve Aplasia: The EMPES Protocol (Early Implantation, Modiolar Proximity, and Early Switch-On).
abstract: Objective To evaluate the efficacy of EMPES [Early implantation, Modiolar Proximity (MP), and Early Switch-on] approach in bilateral cochlear nerve (CN) aplasia. Study design Retrospective cohort study. Setting Tertiary referral center. Patients Forty-six children (86 ears) with bilateral CN aplasia underwent cochlear implantation (CI) between 2011 and 2024 at 2 tertiary centers. Intervention For electrophysiological comparison, CI was performed using CI24RE-CA electrodes without pull-back (conventional implantation) or a slim modiolar electrode with pull-back (better MP). For speech outcome comparison, the conventional approach group comprised conventional implantation cases with ≥12-month follow-up, and the EMPES approach group comprised those in the better MP group implanted before 12 months and followed for ≥12 months. Main outcome measures Mechanistic endpoint, intraoperative ECAP positivity; functional endpoint: longitudinal Categories of Auditory Performance (CAP) scores up to 48 months. Results The better MP group showed higher intraoperative ECAP positivity, which translated into better postoperative outcomes. The EMPES approach demonstrated clear superiority in auditory performance up to 12 months [CAP score 3.00 (2.00 to 4.00) vs. 1.50 (1.00 to 2.25); P=0.010], with significantly fewer poor responders (CAP<2) at 1 year, and maintained narrower variability in median CAP scores through 36 months, indicating more stable auditory progress compared with the conventional approach. No clear association was observed between MRI-based CN aplasia severity and either ECAP positivity or audiological outcomes. Conclusions The EMPES approach improves postoperative audiological outcomes during critical language periods and is recommended for bilateral CN aplasia to enhance language development and potentially reduce the need for auditory brainstem implantation.

title: Computed Tomography-Derived Psoas Muscle Quantity, Attenuation, and 1 Year Mortality in Venovenous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation.
abstract: Computed tomography (CT)-derived skeletal muscle characteristics may provide prognostic information in patients receiving venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV ECMO), but the relative contributions of muscle quantity and attenuation remain uncertain. We retrospectively studied adults who received VV ECMO for severe respiratory failure between 2014 and 2023 and underwent abdominal CT within 48 h before ECMO initiation. Psoas muscle index (PMI) and attenuation were measured using an artificial intelligence-based pipeline, and combined PMI-attenuation phenotypes were evaluated for 1 year mortality. Among 92 patients, 53 (57.6%) died within 1 year. In Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, sex, and initial Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score and stratified by bridge-to-transplantation status, higher PMI (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] per standard deviation increase, 0.58; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.41-0.82) and higher attenuation (aHR per 5 Hounsfield unit increase, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.77-0.97) were associated with lower 1 year mortality. When modeled simultaneously, PMI remained significant, whereas attenuation did not. The low PMI/low attenuation phenotype had the highest mortality risk (aHR, 5.30; 95% CI, 2.10-13.34). PMI showed a more robust association with 1 year mortality, while combined PMI-attenuation phenotyping may identify a particularly high-risk subgroup.

title: Suspected Small Bowel Bleeding: A Single-Center Retrospective Study on Long-Term Prognosis and Predictive Factors.
abstract: Goals We identified prognostic factors for mortality after Suspected small bowel bleeding (SSBB) and evaluated the impact of severe anemia and other clinical factors on patient survival. Background SSBB is characterized by an inability to identify the cause of bleeding despite esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy. Study This retrospective observational study included patients aged ≥20 years with SSBB who underwent capsule endoscopy (CE) at Hokkaido University Hospital in Japan from April 2015 to March 2022. Patient characteristics, blood transfusion history, CE results, blood test results, and post-CE mortality events were collected from electronic medical records. Results CE was performed in 99 patients to investigate the causes of SSBB, identifying bleeding sources in 40.4%. Over a median follow-up of 35 months (range: 0 to 94), mortality occurred in 34 cases. The overall 3-year survival rate was 71.1%. Multivariate analysis identified hemoglobin levels <8.0 g/dL [hazard ratio ( HR )=9.75; 95% CI: 1.26-75.15; P =0.003] and end-stage cancer ( HR =4.94; 95% CI: 2.02-12.10; P <0.001) as independent prognostic factors for mortality after CE for SSBB. Even after excluding patients with small bowel tumors and end-stage cancer, hemoglobin levels <8.0 g/dL ( HR =5.07; 95% CI: 1.10-23.03; P =0.037) remained an independent predictor of mortality. The overall 5-year survival rates for patients without small bowel tumors and end-stage cancer in the groups with hemoglobin levels of ≥8.0 g/dL and <8.0 g/dL were 89.0% and 56.8%, respectively. Conclusion Hemoglobin levels <8.0 g/dL significantly predict mortality in patients with SSBB.

title: Parsonage-turner syndrome: a pulmonologist's guide to the forgotten diaphragm.
abstract: Purpose of review Parsonage-Turner syndrome (PTS), or neuralgic amyotrophy, is framed as a shoulder disorder owned by neurology, and that framing has cost pulmonologists patients. Roughly 1 in 13 develops phrenic neuropathy, and many patients referred for unexplained dyspnea, orthopnea, or rapid eye movement (REM)-predominant sleep-disordered breathing have an undiagnosed, treatable inflammatory neuropathy. This review reframes PTS for pulmonologists. Recent findings Three developments have reshaped practice. High-resolution neuromuscular ultrasound and MR neurography now identify the hourglass constrictions and fascicular entwinement of PTS at the bedside, including in the phrenic nerve. COVID-19 infection and SARS-CoV-2 vaccination produced a global cluster, expanding the phenotype toward bilateral and respiratory-predominant disease. Large Dutch cohort data have replaced anecdote with structure: roughly 60% of patients with phrenic involvement recover meaningfully within 2 years, while the remainder respond best to early noninvasive ventilation and, in refractory cases, diaphragmatic plication. Summary Every pulmonologist evaluating unexplained dyspnea, disproportionate orthopnea, or REM-predominant hypopneas should ask one question: was there severe shoulder or neck pain in the weeks before the breathing changed? If yes, screen with upright and supine spirometry and diaphragm ultrasound. The diagnosis is reachable in a single visit, the immunomodulation window is short, and the cost of missing it is years of avoidable disability.

title: Clinical curative effect of B-ultrasound-guided minimally invasive percutaneous nephrolithotomy and its influences on stone clearance rate in patients with complex kidney stones.
abstract: This study compares short-term perioperative and early postoperative outcomes of B-ultrasound-guided minimally invasive percutaneous nephrolithotomy (MPCNL) and retroperitoneal laparoscopic pyelolithotomy (RLP) in patients with complex kidney stones. This single-center retrospective observational cohort included 120 eligible patients treated between December 2020 and December 2023. Patients were classified according to the treatment actually received (RLP, n = 60; B-ultrasound-guided MPCNL, n = 60); no random allocation was performed. Outcomes included perioperative indicators, 24-hour visual analog scale pain score, 48-hour inflammatory and renal biomarkers, early ultrasound-defined stone clearance at postoperative day 1, and in-hospital complications. Operation time, intraoperative blood loss, and length of hospital stay were lower in the MPCNL group than in the RLP group (nominal P < .05). Early ultrasound-defined stone clearance was 91.67% (55/60) versus 78.33% (47/60), corresponding to a risk difference of 13.3 percentage points (95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.2-25.6), a risk ratio of 1.17 (95% CI = 1.00-1.36), and a Pearson chi-square P = .041. This comparison did not meet a conservative Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of 0.0042 for 12 reported endpoints. At 24 hours, visual analog scale scores were lower in the MPCNL group, and at 48 hours, inflammatory and renal biomarkers were lower (nominal P < .05). Complications occurred in 2/60 (3.33%) versus 8/60 (13.33%); because of sparse events, Fisher exact test was used (P = .095; risk ratio = 0.25, 95% CI = 0.06-1.13). B-ultrasound-guided MPCNL was associated with more favorable short-term perioperative and biomarker outcomes and a nominally higher early ultrasound-defined clearance rate than RLP. However, the retrospective nonrandomized design, incomplete baseline adjustment, short follow-up, outcome-measurement limitations, and multiple comparisons preclude causal or long-term effectiveness claims. These findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in adequately powered prospective comparative studies.

title: Artificial intelligence empowering the diagnosis and treatment of rotator cuff tears: A systematic review from image optimization to prognosis prediction.
abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is being developed for image acquisition, quantitative tissue assessment, diagnosis, and clinical prediction in rotator cuff tears. The breadth of this literature and its methodological limitations have not been integrated across the complete care pathway. Methods We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library from inception to July 5, 2026 for English-language original studies applying AI to rotator cuff-related reconstruction, segmentation or quantitative imaging, diagnosis or classification, anatomical measurement, or prognosis. Two reviewers screened reports and extracted study, data, model, validation, reference standard, and performance characteristics. Diagnostic accuracy studies were assessed with QUADAS-2 and prediction-model studies with PROBAST. Because clinical tasks, modalities, models, reference standards, and reported metrics were not sufficiently comparable, evidence was synthesized narratively rather than pooled statistically. Results Sixty-six reports were included: 35 diagnostic accuracy or classification studies, 20 segmentation or quantitative imaging studies, 9 prognosis or outcome prediction studies, 1 Magnetic Resonance Imaging reconstruction or image-optimization study, and 1 exploratory unsupervised-phenotyping study. Applications spanned Magnetic Resonance Imaging, radiography, ultrasound, computed tomography, clinical or multimodal data, motion video, and emerging sensing data. QUADAS-2 classified overall risk-of-bias as high in 27/36 diagnostic studies, unclear in 6/36, and low in 3/36. PROBAST classified all 8/8 completed prediction-model studies as high risk-of-bias; 1 protocol without model results was not rated. Promising internal performance was recurrent, but selection methods, imperfect or incompletely described reference standards, limited external validation, small or selected datasets, and analysis-stage weaknesses constrained clinical inference. Conclusion AI has proof-of-concept value across rotator cuff imaging and decision support, but the current evidence does not establish routine clinical readiness or replacement of clinician judgment. Prospective multicenter studies, transparent reference standards, independent external validation, calibration and clinical-utility assessment, and standardized task-specific reporting are required.

AI has proof-of-concept value across rotator cuff imaging and decision support, but the current evidence does not establish routine clinical readiness or replacement of clinician judgment. Prospective multicenter studies, transparent reference standards, independent external validation, calibration and clinical-utility assessment, and standardized task-specific reporting are required.

title: Cholecystogastric fistula masquerading as gastrointestinal stromal tumour: Unusual presentation of gallbladder adenomyomatosis - a case report.
abstract: Rationale We present the case of gallbladder adenomyomatosis (GA)-induced cholecystogastric fistula (CGF) that mimicked an invasive gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), leading to diagnostic and surgical challenges in an emergency setting. Patient concerns A 71-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with acute abdominal pain and clinical signs of mechanical small-bowel obstruction (SBO). Diagnoses Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed a 6-cm mass along the gastric antrum with apparent hepatic invasion and concurrent features of SBO. The gallbladder was not visualized. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) demonstrated a subepithelial tumor-like bulge with a small mucosal opening in the gastric antrum, raising suspicion of a fistulous tract. Interventions Emergency exploratory laparotomy identified two phytobezoars in the small bowel, which were treated by segmental resection and primary anastomosis. The gastric mass was found to be densely adherent to the liver, and bile leakage was encountered during dissection, prompting intraoperative hepatobiliary consultation. Outcomes Histopathological examination of the resected specimen confirmed GA with inflammatory granulation tissue at the gallbladder-gastric serosal interface, with no evidence of malignancy. The patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged 29 days postoperatively. Lessons This case highlights a novel and clinically significant diagnostic pitfall: GA-induced CGF can convincingly simulate an invasive gastric neoplasm on multimodal imaging and endoscopy. Recognition of biliary red flags, including non-visualization of the gallbladder on CT, a mucosal opening adjacent to a subepithelial-appearing lesion on EGD, and intramural cystic foci on imaging, is essential for accurate preoperative diagnosis.

title: Challenges in glaucoma diagnosis in small optic discs: An OCT-based analysis.
abstract: This study aimed to assess how optic disc (OD) size influences structural and functional tests in patients with glaucoma with small and normal-sized discs and to compare the sensitivities of these tests. The study comprised 182 eyes, including 109 eyes of 73 patients diagnosed with glaucoma and 73 eyes of 41 healthy subjects. Eyes were classified according to OD size as either small (<1.6 mm2) or normal (1.6-2.1 mm2). Optic nerve head parameters, peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness, and macular ganglion cell analysis were assessed using Cirrus 4000 spectral-domain optical coherence tomography. The sensitivities of RNFL, macular ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer (GCIPL), and visual field parameters were evaluated using logistic receiver operating characteristic regression analysis. The mean ages of the patients and controls were 65.48 ± 7.94 years and 65.22 ± 6.55 years, respectively (P = .859). The mean disc diameter was 1.48 ± 0.11 mm in the small-disc group and 1.86 ± 0.16 mm in the normal-disc group. The mean deviation values were -5.52 ± 4.81 and -4.54 ± 3.73 in the small- and normal-disc groups, respectively (P = .268). Among patients with glaucoma and small ODs, GCIPL parameters (mean, minimum, superior, and inferior hemifield values) demonstrated greater sensitivity than RNFL parameters. In contrast, RNFL parameters (average, superior, inferior, and corresponding hemifield values) showed greater sensitivity than GCIPL parameters in patients with normal-sized ODs. Macular structural parameters demonstrated higher sensitivity for glaucoma diagnosis in patients with small ODs. However, a comprehensive assessment integrating both macular and peripapillary structural parameters may improve diagnostic accuracy by providing complementary information in these patients.

title: The role of total vaginal hysterectomy versus total abdominal hysterectomy in surgical management of uterine myomas: A retrospective single center cohort study.
abstract: Total vaginal hysterectomy (TVH) has been performed even for enlarged uterine myoma, but it is regarded as more inferior than total abdominal hysterectomy (TAH). The aim of this study was to compare the role of surgical choice in patients undergoing either TVH or TAH for uterine myoma. In this retrospective cohort study, 140 hysterectomies with bilateral adnexectomy were planned for postmenopausal women with uterine myoma between 2020 and 2024, in a tertiary center hospital. The diagnosis was established after clinical symptomatology and transvaginal ultrasound, with histopathological confirmation obtained postoperatively. The patients were divided into 2 groups: the TVH group (n = 70) and the TAH group (n = 70). Patient features such as age, uterine weight, body mass index (BMI), parity, operative time, intraoperative blood loss, hospital stay, medical history, surgical history, intra and postoperative complications, and adhesions were assessed. Mean age, uterine weight, BMI, and parity showed no significant difference between the groups. Instead, the TVH group was linked with significantly shorter operative time, lower intraoperative blood loss, and reduced hospital stay compared to the TAH group (P < .001). However, there were more medical and surgical histories in patients from the TAH group compared with the TVH group, including postoperative complications (11.44% vs 4.29%) and adhesions (32.86% vs 20%). In most cases, uterine hemisection, tactical myomectomy, or morcellation were used in order to reduce uterine size for the TVH group (78.57%). Our findings sustain that shorter operating time, lower intraoperative blood loss, and reduced hospital stay recommend TVH as a suitable choice in carefully selected postmenopausal women with enlarged uterine myoma.

title: Diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis: A bibliometric review from 2008 to 2024.
abstract: Background The pathogenesis and pathological progression of ankylosing spondylitis (AS) remain unclear. Owing to the absence of a gold standard for diagnosing AS, diagnostic delays are frequently encountered in clinical practice, exacerbating the disease burden. In the past 16 years, several diagnostic studies on AS have been published. This study aimed to summarize the developmental trends and frontier hotspots in AS diagnosis through a bibliometric review. Methods Data were extracted from English publications on AS diagnosis from the Web of Science Core Collection (January 1, 2008-October 21, 2024). CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and the Biblioshiny R package were used to analyze the overview of the publication output, countries/regions, institutions, authors, sources, references, and keywords. Results A total of 1205 articles from 396 journals across 65 countries were included. The highest annual output occurred in 2021 (n = 111, 9.21%), whereas 2015 had the highest average number of citations (n = 5.1). Clinical Rheumatology (n = 76, 6.31%) was the most influential journal. China (n = 244, 20.25%), Berlin Institute of Health (n = 116, 9.63%), and Sieper J (n = 28, 2.32%) ranked first in terms of country, institution, and author productivity, respectively. The top 3 reference clusters were "diagnostic criteria," "therapeutics," and "recommendations." Burst detection identified 4 emerging post-2021 keywords: "children," "cells," "spondyloarthritis," and "expression." Conclusion AS diagnosis research has evolved through a growth phase (2008-2021), followed by a transitional or reorientation phase (2022-2024). Magnetic resonance imaging, Mendelian randomization, and biomarkers are current hotspots; Mendelian randomization serves as an etiological adjunct with the potential to inform biomarker discovery, though its findings do not yet constitute diagnostic tools. The apparent slowdown in recent years largely reflects evolving terminology (AS vs radiographic axial spondyloarthritis) and bibliometric time-lag bias rather than true intellectual stagnation, alongside fragmented pathophysiological insights and a lack of specific clinical features.

title: Androgen insensitivity syndrome: A case report.
abstract: Rationale 46, XY disorder of sex development (46, XY DSD) is relatively rare and frequently missed in clinical practice, necessitating early standardized diagnosis and treatment. Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS), a major subtype, should be considered in phenotypic females with suggestive clinical clues. Patient concerns A 29-year-old phenotypic female presented with primary amenorrhea and intermittent abdominal pain. Examination revealed normal breast development, sparse pubic hair, and female external genitalia. Pelvic ultrasonography and CT showed an absent uterus and ovaries, with bilateral inguinal masses. Diagnoses The case met the 3 diagnostic criteria for 46, XY DSD: 46,XY karyotype, testicular tissue, and feminized external genitalia. A diagnosis clinically consistent with complete AIS was further supported by the characteristic phenotype - female appearance, normal breast development, sparse pubic hair, and absent Müllerian structures. Other etiologies of undervirilization, including 5α-reductase deficiency and 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency, were considered. Genetic confirmation was unavailable, limiting subtype certainty. Interventions Following counseling, the patient underwent laparoscopic bilateral orchiectomy as prophylactic gonadectomy to reduce malignancy risk, together with inguinal hernia repair, followed by postoperative hormone replacement therapy. Postoperative histopathology confirmed testicular tissue with Leydig cell hyperplasia, absent spermatogenic cells, and no malignancy. Outcomes Abdominal pain resolved postoperatively, with improved psychological well-being and adaptation to the diagnosis under ongoing endocrine and psychological support. Lessons 46, XY DSD is underdiagnosed due to phenotypic variability, reliance on specialized tests, and social biases. AIS should be considered in the differential diagnosis of phenotypic females presenting with primary amenorrhea, developed secondary sexual characteristics, and an absent uterus on ultrasound. However, definitive subtyping requires AR gene sequencing, which was not available in this case. Early diagnosis requires careful assessment of newborn external genitalia, with specialist evaluation prompted by any atypical findings, and hormonal and genetic testing in adolescents with abnormal development. Multidisciplinary care - involving gynecologists, endocrinologists, surgeons, geneticists, and mental-health professionals - is essential for comprehensive management, including psychological support, hormone therapy, and timely prophylactic gonadectomy. Establishing specialized multidisciplinary centers for DSD is also recommended.

title: Pulmonary cryptococcosis mimicking metastatic progression despite systemic disease stability in advanced colon cancer: A case report and literature review.
abstract: Rationale In patients with advanced cancer, newly detected pulmonary nodules are often interpreted as metastatic progression. The distinctive feature of this case was the appearance of multiple new lung nodules during otherwise controlled systemic disease: the primary colonic lesion and hepatic metastases remained stable while tumor marker levels declined. This radiologic-clinical discordance prompted reconsideration of metastatic progression and broadened the differential diagnosis. Patient concerns A patient with advanced colon cancer, who was undergoing systemic chemotherapy and had otherwise stable disease, was found to have developed new pulmonary nodules on routine surveillance imaging. The patient was entirely asymptomatic from a respiratory standpoint. The primary clinical concern was the discordance between the radiologically suspicious findings and the patient's overall stable clinical condition. Diagnoses The initial radiologic impression favored pulmonary metastases. However, multidisciplinary review recognized the discordance between the new lung lesions and the otherwise stable systemic disease and raised concern for an opportunistic infection. Serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan and qualitative cryptococcal capsular polysaccharide antigen tests were positive, supporting a diagnosis of pulmonary cryptococcosis. Interventions After cerebrospinal fluid evaluation excluded central nervous system involvement, fluconazole 400 mg once daily was initiated. The anticancer strategy was not escalated on the basis of the pulmonary findings alone. Outcomes Follow-up chest computed tomography demonstrated marked regression of the pulmonary nodules. Lessons When new pulmonary lesions arise despite stability or response at established tumor sites, apparent radiologic progression should not automatically be equated with oncologic progression. Integrating the longitudinal treatment response, tumor marker trends, clinical symptoms, imaging features, and targeted infectious testing can prevent unnecessary changes in cancer therapy and may avoid invasive procedures when a sufficiently supported alternative diagnosis is available.

title: Biodegradable pins fixation for lateral condylar fracture of the humerus in children: A retrospective study of biodegradable pin fixation combined with versus without absorbable tension band wiring.
abstract: Biodegradable pins are increasingly used in the treatment of lateral condylar fractures of the humerus (LCFH) in children, but the strength of the biodegradable pin is weaker than that of K-wire. However, to enhance the stability of LCFH fixed by biodegradable pins, absorbable tension band wiring is often combined with the application, yet high-quality comparative evidence verifying the clinical value of this auxiliary reinforcement remains lacking. This study aimed to compare and analyze whether auxiliary absorbable tension band wiring has clinical significance for Weiss type III LCFH and to clarify whether additional tension band fixation is clinically necessary in reducing postoperative complications and improving fracture stability. This study enrolled 96 children with Weiss type III LCFH admitted between January 2017 and September 2019. The patients were divided into 2 groups: A (fixed by 3 biodegradable pins alone, n = 45) and B (fixed by 3 biodegradable pins and combined with the application of absorbable figure-of-eight tension band wiring, n = 51). Preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative indicators, including age, sex, operation time, intraoperative blood loss, fracture healing time, elbow functional recovery time, and postoperative complications, were compared between the 2 groups. Postoperative elbow function was assessed by using the Flynn grading system. All radiographic measurements and functional evaluations were performed by 2 calibrated orthopedic surgeons with excellent inter-rater reliability. Sample size calculations were performed before data collection to guarantee statistical validity. There were no significant differences in age, sex, injured side, preoperative fracture displacement, operation duration, intraoperative blood loss, fracture healing time, elbow functional recovery time, or Flynn functional grading (all P > .05). Complete fracture union was observed in all patients, and no adverse complications, such as wound infection, bone nonunion, osteonecrosis, or elbow deformity, occurred in either group. Absorbable tension band wiring reinforcement is not required after biodegradable pin fixation in the treatment of LCFH in children.

title: Suspected allergic bronchopulmonary candidiasis in a patient with concurrent multidrug-resistant bacterial pneumonia: A case report.
abstract: Rationale Allergic bronchopulmonary candidiasis (ABPC) is a rare pulmonary hypersensitivity disorder; diagnosis is difficult because Candida albicans is usually a respiratory commensal. Patient concerns A 70-year-old man with hypertension and prior cerebral infarction was admitted for sudden right limb weakness (6.5 hours) and diagnosed with hemorrhagic cerebral infarction in the intensive care unit. Diagnoses Persistent fever and pulmonary infiltrates developed despite broad-spectrum antibiotics. Total immunoglobulin E (IgE) was 2181 IU/mL; sputum grew C albicans + carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid metagenomic next-generation sequencing detected C albicans, P aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, EBV, and HSV-1. ABPC was suspected alongside multidrug-resistant bacterial pneumonia. Interventions Ceftazidime-avibactam (2.5 g q8h) + nebulized polymyxin B (0.5 M IU q12h); oral voriconazole (400 mg q12h loading, then 200 mg q12h); IV methylprednisolone 40 mg/d. Outcomes Clinical improvement on combined therapy; respiratory stabilization within 2 weeks; intensive care unit transfer out. Follow-up chest computed tomography showed resolution of infiltrates; total IgE fell from 2181 to 995 IU/mL (-54%). Discharged with hemorrhagic cerebral infarction, hypertension, carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas pneumonia, K pneumoniae co-infection, and ABPM. Lessons Persistent infiltrates with high IgE and Candida isolation should suggest ABPM, not intensified antibiotics. ABPC can occur in older patients without asthma. Early corticosteroids plus antifungals yield rapid improvement. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing complements conventional testing but cannot confirm ABPC alone.

title: Primary pulmonary mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma presenting as a right hilar mass: A case report.
abstract: Rationale Primary pulmonary lymphoma (PPL) is an extremely rare malignant lung tumor that is frequently misdiagnosed as pneumonia or lung cancer due to its atypical radiological and clinical presentation. The rationale of this report is to elucidate the diagnostic value of combining computed tomography (CT) and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) in evaluating a rare presentation of PPL. Patient concerns A 44-year-old male was admitted after an incidental lung lesion was discovered during routine screening. He was completely asymptomatic, lacking respiratory or systemic "B symptoms." Diagnoses A baseline chest CT identified a 3.9 × 3.5 cm soft-tissue mass in the right hilar region that compressed the right upper lobe bronchus, leading to secondary post-obstructive consolidation that lacked the characteristic air bronchogram sign. The CT also revealed an incidental 2.6 × 2.6 cm anterior mediastinal nodule. Subsequent whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated intense tracer uptake in the right hilar mass with a maximum standardized uptake value of 7.1 and mild-to-moderate uptake in an adjacent regional lymph node (maximum standardized uptake value of 3.2). The scan showed completely absent uptake in the anterior mediastinal nodule and the post-obstructive consolidation, arguing against metabolically active malignancy in those areas. Histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis from a bronchoscopic transbronchial lung biopsy confirmed primary pulmonary mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma. Interventions The patient underwent localized radiotherapy targeting the right hilar mass and the FDG-avid regional hilar/posterior mediastinal lymph node. A total dose of 66 Gy was delivered in 18 fractions over the course of 3 weeks. Outcomes At the 2-month post-discharge follow-up, a repeat chest CT revealed a marked reduction in the size of both the hilar lesion and the regional lymph nodes. The patient remained completely asymptomatic, and his laboratory parameters normalized. Lessons Differentiating PPL from central lung cancer and coexisting benign mediastinal abnormalities presents a significant clinical challenge, particularly when atypical radiological features mimic aggressive carcinomas. Whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT serves as an invaluable, noninvasive modality for metabolic characterization, accurate loco-regional staging, and preventing clinical overstaging by effectively differentiating metabolically active lymphoma from concurrent benign lesions.

title: Excellent response to high-dose Riboflavin in Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome: A case report.
abstract: Rationale Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome, currently recognized within the spectrum of riboflavin transporter deficiency type 3 (RTD3), is a rare inherited neurometabolic disorder associated with pathogenic variants in SLC52A3. It typically presents with progressive sensorineural hearing loss, pontobulbar dysfunction, peripheral neuropathy, and respiratory involvement. Diagnosis may be delayed because routine metabolic and neuromuscular investigations can be unrevealing despite a characteristic clinical phenotype. Patient concerns A young Asian man presented with several years of progressive bilateral hearing loss followed by worsening dysphagia to solids and liquids, symmetrical limb weakness, muscle wasting, and acute-on-chronic dyspnea. Two siblings had previously died at a young age after developing a similar sequence of hearing impairment, dysphagia, limb weakness, and unexplained respiratory failure. Diagnoses Neurological examination showed tongue atrophy with fasciculations, thenar wasting, bifacial weakness, mild ptosis, diminished gag reflex, and symmetrical limb weakness. Audiometry confirmed profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Nerve conduction studies demonstrated predominantly motor axonal neuropathy, while electromyography showed chronic and active denervation. Repetitive nerve stimulation, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, magnetic resonance imaging, creatine kinase levels, and metabolic investigations were unrevealing. Targeted genetic testing detected pathogenic SLC52A3 variants, confirming RTD3/ Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome. Interventions High-dose oral riboflavin was initiated empirically at 40 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses before genetic confirmation because of progressive respiratory compromise and strong clinical suspicion. Supportive management included nutritional support and nocturnal noninvasive ventilation with bilevel positive airway pressure. Outcomes The patient showed marked improvement after riboflavin initiation. Respiratory effort improved within several days, and forced vital capacity increased from 35% to 50% of predicted within 1 week. Limb strength improved, and by 8 weeks the patient had gained 3 kg with stabilization of dysphagia and improved oral intake. At 6 months, neurological status remained stable without further electrophysiological progression. Riboflavin was well tolerated. Lessons RTD3 should be considered in young patients with progressive sensorineural hearing loss associated with bulbar dysfunction, motor neuropathy, or respiratory weakness, particularly when family history is suggestive. Recognition of the characteristic phenotype, targeted genetic testing, and prompt initiation of high-dose riboflavin may substantially alter the clinical course of this potentially treatable disorder.

title: Concordance of p16 status between US-guided core needle biopsy and surgical specimens in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma: A diagnostic accuracy study.
abstract: With the increasing prevalence of human papillomavirus (HPV)-driven oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC), there is a need for efficient, minimally invasive methods to evaluate p16 status. This study aimed to assess the concordance of p16 status between ultrasound (US)-guided core needle biopsy (CNB) of cervical lymph nodes and surgical specimens, and to describe the numbers of CNB and surgical sessions required to establish the histopathologic diagnosis. This retrospective study included 39 patients diagnosed with OPSCC or head and neck squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary (SCCUP) at a single tertiary hospital between March 2019 and March 2024. All included patients underwent US-guided CNB of cervical lymph nodes and a surgical procedure (biopsy or resection), and had evaluable p16 immunohistochemistry (IHC) results on both specimen types. The concordance rate for p16 status between US-guided CNB and surgical specimens was 100.0% (39/39; 95% CI, 91.0-100.0%; 35 p16-positive and 4 p16-negative cases). Sensitivity was 100.0% (35/35; 95% CI, 90.0-100.0%) and specificity was 100.0% (4/4; 95% CI, 39.8-100.0%). In all 39 included patients, a diagnosis of metastatic squamous cell carcinoma and an evaluable p16 result were obtained at the first CNB session. Among the 35 patients with OPSCC, 10 (28.6%) required more than 1 surgical session at the primary tumor site. No immediate complications were observed following US-guided CNB. In this cohort, US-guided CNB of cervical lymph nodes showed complete observed concordance with surgical specimens for p16 status, and a diagnosis with an evaluable p16 result was obtained at the first CNB session in all patients. Prospective, multicenter validation including more p16-negative cases is required before wider adoption.

title: Outcomes of sequential keratoplasty for bilateral gelatinous drop-like corneal dystrophy: A case report.
abstract: Rationale Gelatinous drop-like corneal dystrophy (GDLD) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by subepithelial amyloid deposition, progressive corneal opacification, and recurrent erosions. GDLD may present during the first decade of life and interfere with visual development. It may recur after keratoplasty, complicating surgical management. Patient concerns A 21-year-old woman of Yemeni ancestry, living in a remote area with limited access to corneal transplantation, presented with progressive left eye visual decline and foreign body sensation since early childhood. She had long-standing bilateral visual impairment and a positive family history. Her first surgery was right eye penetrating keratoplasty (PK), performed elsewhere approximately 1 year earlier for an undiagnosed opacity. Diagnoses Examination revealed nystagmus, a clear right graft with yellowish recipient deposits, and dense limbus-to-limbus left corneal opacification with stromal haze, mulberry-like deposits, and neovascularization. Uncorrected visual acuity (VA) was 20/200 in the right eye and counting fingers in the left. Best spectacle-corrected VA was 20/100 in the right eye, while reliable refraction could not be obtained in the left. Histopathology demonstrated Congo red-positive subepithelial amyloid deposits with birefringence under polarized light, confirming GDLD. Genetic testing for tumor-associated calcium signal transducer 2 was not performed. Interventions The left eye underwent superficial keratectomy and attempted lamellar dissection assisted by intraoperative optical coherence tomography; dense deep stromal opacity necessitated conversion to full-thickness PK. Outcomes Both grafts remained clear without rejection during follow-up. Minimal focal subepithelial haze in a temporal area of the left donor graft was noted at the 2 most recent visits, remained stationary between them, and was clinically insignificant. At final follow-up, approximately 2 years after right eye PK and 10 months after left eye PK, best spectacle-corrected VA was 20/100 in the right eye and 20/80 - 1 in the left. Intraocular pressure was normal, and posterior pole examinations were unremarkable. Lessons Advanced bilateral GDLD poses clinical and surgical challenges. PK may restore corneal clarity and provide meaningful visual rehabilitation, although recovery may remain incomplete after early-onset visual impairment and delayed treatment. Long-term monitoring is essential because recurrence and repeat intervention may be required. Early recognition, timely referral, and individualized management matter where donor corneal tissue access is limited.
