title: Breast Cancer Screening in Pregnant and Lactating Patients: A Practical Approach.
abstract: Screening and diagnostic evaluation for breast cancer is increasingly common during pregnancy and lactation due to delayed childbearing and identification of elevated hereditary and familial risk during reproductive years, with patients often undergoing risk assessment beginning at 25 years of age. Although mammography is safe for pregnant and lactating patients, its sensitivity may be reduced because hormonal changes increase parenchymal density and can obscure malignant lesions. US is widely used because it does not involve exposure to ionizing radiation and serves as the primary modality for evaluating symptomatic patients. However, its role in routine screening remains uncertain because evidence regarding screening performance and outcomes in pregnant and lactating populations is limited. MRI is contraindicated during pregnancy but may be performed during lactation for screening of patients at high risk for or with newly diagnosed breast cancer, despite its pronounced background parenchymal enhancement. Timely evaluation of breast symptoms and imaging abnormalities is critical given the rising incidence of pregnancy-associated breast cancer and the potential for delayed diagnosis. Therefore, radiologists must balance diagnostic performance with maternal and fetal safety when selecting imaging modalities. The authors review the current American College of Radiology Appropriateness Criteria and the guidelines of other professional organizations; summarize the epidemiology of pregnancy-associated breast cancer and the physiologic breast changes that affect imaging interpretation; and highlight modality-specific limitations, safety considerations, and contraindications. Strategies for identifying patients at high risk for breast cancer who require continued screening and for effectively communicating imaging risks, benefits, and expectations to patients and referring clinicians are also discussed.

title: Opportunistic CT Screening: Clinical Applications, Technical Foundations, and Best Practices.
abstract: Opportunistic CT screening refers to the extraction of clinically relevant imaging biomarkers from CT examinations routinely performed for unrelated primary indications. This screening does not require additional radiation exposure, imaging time, or patient burden. Advances in automated image analysis and artificial intelligence (AI) have substantially expanded the feasibility of opportunistic CT screening across a range of conditions, including low bone mineral density, hepatic steatosis, sarcopenia, adiposity, and vascular calcifications. These biomarkers are increasingly being recognized as important contributors to fracture risk, cardiometabolic disease, and frailty; yet they often remain undiagnosed in routine clinical practice. While numerous studies have demonstrated technical feasibility and diagnostic performance, widespread clinical adoption of opportunistic CT screening remains limited. Key challenges include those related to workflow integration, standardization of measurement techniques, quality assurance, interpretability of results, and uncertainty regarding downstream clinical management and value. In particular, not all opportunistic imaging biomarkers are equally actionable, and inappropriate or indiscriminate reporting may contribute to overdiagnosis or unnecessary follow-up. The authors summarize common applications of opportunistic CT screening, highlighting typical imaging findings and biomarkers. The authors discuss the evolution of automated and AI-based approaches, with emphasis on practical considerations for deployment, including pre- and postdeployment quality assurance, algorithm monitoring, and practical considerations for clinical integration. Emerging applications also are reviewed, with attention to current limitations. With a focus on clinical integration, this review is intended to inform radiologists, informaticians, and others working in health care systems who seek to translate opportunistic CT screening from proof-of-concept studies into scalable, clinically meaningful practice.

title: Surveillance for Hepatocellular Carcinoma in Patients at High Risk.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the third leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide and most often arises in patients with chronic liver disease and cirrhosis. Since curative treatment options are largely limited to early-stage disease, effective surveillance strategies are essential to improve outcomes. Current guidelines recommend semiannual US combined with serum α-fetoprotein level testing as the standard surveillance approach for most patients at high risk. Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System 2024 guidance provides a structured framework for interpretation of surveillance US and highlights the importance of examination quality assessment and reporting by incorporating it into the management decision-making algorithm. US surveillance improves early tumor detection and survival but demonstrates suboptimal sensitivity in certain high-risk subgroups, particularly patients with obesity, hepatic steatosis, and advanced cirrhosis. Growing evidence supports the use of alternative strategies including biomarker panel results and abbreviated MRI protocols in selected patient subgroups because these approaches demonstrate higher sensitivity and favorable cost-effectiveness when applied to appropriately risk-stratified populations. Furthermore, cost-effectiveness analyses consistently indicate that surveillance efficiency strongly depends on individual HCC risk, imaging costs, surveillance use, and societal willingness-to-pay thresholds, supporting a departure from uniform "one-size-fits-all" strategies in favor of personalized, risk-adapted surveillance paradigms. Despite advances in diagnostic performance, surveillance use remains suboptimal in clinical practice due to patient-, provider-, and system-level barriers. The authors aim to synthesize current evidence on HCC surveillance including identifying target populations; evaluating the diagnostic performance of available modalities; and considering cost-effectiveness, emerging technologies, and real-world barriers to implementation of surveillance protocols.

Current guidelines recommend semiannual US combined with serum α-fetoprotein level testing as the standard surveillance approach for most patients at high risk. Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System 2024 guidance provides a structured framework for interpretation of surveillance US and highlights the importance of examination quality assessment and reporting by incorporating it into the management decision-making algorithm. US surveillance improves early tumor detection and survival but demonstrates suboptimal sensitivity in certain high-risk subgroups, particularly patients with obesity, hepatic steatosis, and advanced cirrhosis. Growing evidence supports the use of alternative strategies including biomarker panel results and abbreviated MRI protocols in selected patient subgroups because these approaches demonstrate higher sensitivity and favorable cost-effectiveness when applied to appropriately risk-stratified populations. Furthermore, cost-effectiveness analyses consistently indicate that surveillance efficiency strongly depends on individual HCC risk, imaging costs, surveillance use, and societal willingness-to-pay thresholds, supporting a departure from uniform "one-size-fits-all" strategies in favor of personalized, risk-adapted surveillance paradigms. Despite advances in diagnostic performance, surveillance use remains suboptimal in clinical practice due to patient-, provider-, and system-level barriers. The authors aim to synthesize current evidence on HCC surveillance including identifying target populations; evaluating the diagnostic performance of available modalities; and considering cost-effectiveness, emerging technologies, and real-world barriers to implementation of surveillance protocols.

title: Lung Cancer Screening: Beyond Pulmonary Nodules.
abstract: Low-dose CT lung cancer screening reduces lung cancer mortality in individuals at high risk and frequently reveals clinically relevant incidental findings. In the National Lung Screening Trial, approximately one-third of screening CT examinations demonstrated abnormalities other than lung cancer, raising challenges related to interpretation, reporting, and further management. The absence of consistent guidance and the variable clinical significance of these findings may hinder the broader adoption of lung cancer screening. Opportunistic screening leverages low-dose CT examinations performed for lung cancer detection to identify additional serious conditions at no extra cost, radiation exposure, or patient burden. The authors provide a practical framework for recognizing, reporting, and managing common opportunistic findings on lung cancer screening CT images, with an emphasis on evidence-based recommendations and current professional society guidance. Key thoracic findings include emphysema, interstitial lung abnormalities, interstitial lung disease, coronary artery calcification, thoracic aortic aneurysm, and pulmonary artery enlargement. Each of these findings, if unrecognized, is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Extrapulmonary findings such as low bone density and lesions found incidentally in the upper abdominal organs further expand the clinical value of lung cancer screening. The authors highlight standardized visual and quantitative assessment methods, recommended follow-up pathways, and the importance of structured reporting, including appropriate use of the Lung CT Screening Reporting and Data System "S" (other non-lung cancer findings) modifier. Emerging artificial intelligence tools are discussed as critical enablers for scalable opportunistic screening, offering automated detection, quantification, and longitudinal assessment of emphysema, coronary calcium levels, vascular dimensions, bone density, body composition, and selected abdominal pathologic conditions. By integrating opportunistic screening into routine lung cancer screening workflows, radiologists can extend the benefit of lung cancer screening with CT beyond cancer detection to facilitate comprehensive risk stratification and preventive care.

title: CT Colonography: Where Are We with Colorectal Cancer Screening?
abstract: CT colonography (CTC) is a validated screening test for detection and prevention of colorectal cancer (CRC). In the United States, screening CTC has been covered for Medicare beneficiaries since 2025, elevating it to equal status with other reimbursed CRC screening tests and ending a 15-year policy stalemate. Screening CTC is a highly accurate examination with an immaculate safety record and equivalent sensitivity to colonoscopy for clinically significant polyps. Long-term observational CTC cohorts confirm safety for established polyp size thresholds in terms of test positivity and screening and surveillance intervals. Excellent technique with cathartic bowel preparation, stool tagging, and colonic distention is necessary for high-quality imaging and interpretation, particularly in detection of flat sessile serrated lesions (SSLs). Large SSLs and adenomatous polyps are the most relevant benign precursor lesions to CRC and are the main target of a primary prevention screening strategy. Only CTC and colonoscopy are sufficiently accurate for primary prevention, whereas stool-based and recently approved blood-based tests are limited to detection of cancer in a shorter screening window. CTC allows for selective polypectomy by risk-stratifying large polyps for removal, surveilling small polyps, and ignoring diminutive lesions. CTC is more efficient at identifying advanced neoplasia compared with a universal polypectomy strategy of colonoscopy only, which removes more pseudodisease and incurs excess risk of colonic perforation without benefit. Despite abundant evidence supporting CTC as an ideal screening test, it suffers from widespread and worsening underutilization due to barriers affecting radiology practice and physician support. Opportunistic screening and national trends in the CRC screening landscape will impact future uptake of CTC.

title: Cancer Predisposition Syndromes in Children: Who, When, and How to Screen?
abstract: Childhood cancer predisposition syndromes (CPSs) are individually rare but collectively account for approximately 15%-20% of pediatric cancers. Advances in genomic testing have identified more than 100 cancer susceptibility genes, enabling earlier recognition of at-risk children and prompting implementation of structured surveillance programs. Imaging is central to screening, which also typically includes physical examination and biochemical testing, guided by the syndrome-specific tumor spectrum, age-related penetrance, tumor growth kinetics, and defined risk thresholds. In general, screening is recommended when the risk of developing a malignancy exceeds 5% within a specified age window. Pediatric CPS surveillance presents unique challenges. Protocols must balance early tumor detection with minimization of potential harm, including cumulative radiation exposure, contrast material-related risks, sedation requirements, and psychosocial burden associated with repeated or lifelong imaging. Ionizing radiation-free modalities, particularly US and MRI, form the backbone of surveillance. Whole-body MRI, with its large field of view and ability to allow assessment of multiple organ systems in a single examination, is increasingly incorporated into surveillance protocols for select syndromes associated with a variety of tumors. Sequence optimization and nonsedative strategies are frequently used to mitigate prolonged acquisition. Familiarity with syndrome-specific tumor imaging characteristics is essential to optimize lesion detection and reduce false-positive and false-negative interpretations. Radiologists may also be the first to recognize characteristic tumors suggestive of an underlying hereditary condition. On the basis of the updated recommendations from the 2023 American Association for Cancer Research pediatric CPS workshop, the authors review outlines guiding principles for surveillance, summarizing imaging components of current protocols for several common or clinically significant childhood CPSs.

title: Screening for Common Gynecologic Malignancies.
abstract: Gynecologic malignancies, including cervical, endometrial, and ovarian cancers (the most common), are a substantial cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide, with the prognosis linked to the stage at diagnosis. The aim of screening is to help detect premalignant or early-stage malignant lesions to reduce mortality. Imaging has a limited role in primary screening for the most common gynecologic cancers and usually enters the patient care workflow after a positive screening test or abnormal laboratory results are obtained. Population-level screening for cervical cancer in individuals at average risk involves cytologic analysis and testing for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), with modified guidelines for patients at increased risk (ie, those with HIV infection, chronic immunosuppression, a history of high-grade cervical dysplasia, prior HPV-related lower genital tract malignancies, or in utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol [DES]). Routine population-level screening for endometrial and ovarian cancers in patients at average risk is not recommended; evaluation is driven by symptoms. Screening for endometrial cancer in patients at risk (eg, those with Lynch syndrome) includes clinical evaluation and assessment of endometrial thickness at transvaginal US. US-based screening for ovarian cancer in individuals at high risk (eg, those with BRCA gene mutations) is reserved for selected patients (eg, those who defer risk-reducing bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy), who undergo transvaginal US screening and serum biomarker level testing. When gynecologic malignancy is suspected based on symptoms, physical examination, or abnormal laboratory results, imaging aids in lesion detection and characterization, staging, treatment planning, and posttreatment surveillance. Imaging findings are increasingly integrated into formal staging systems, including the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics classification system for cervical and endometrial cancer, which highlights the radiologist's role in multidisciplinary care. The authors summarize current and emerging screening strategies for cervical, endometrial, and ovarian cancers and the integration of imaging into the screening workflow. © RSNA, 2026 Supplemental material is available for this article.

title: Targeted US Screening in High-Risk Newborns and Infants: Indications, Techniques, and Disease Findings.
abstract: Newborns and infants with certain perinatal exposures, congenital conditions, and genetic syndromes are at increased risk for clinically significant diseases and may benefit from early detection. In these children, imaging serves as a targeted screening tool to identify actionable abnormalities during a window in which intervention may reduce morbidity and long-term sequelae. The authors summarize evidence-based US screening strategies for high-risk newborns and infants encountered in clinical practice, including preterm infants, newborns with a breech presentation, children with congenital and syndromic conditions, and children with tumor predisposition syndromes. For each group, the authors discuss the rationale for screening, optimal timing, key technical considerations, and imaging findings that directly influence management. Across indications, effective screening follows common principles: risk-based selection rather than universal imaging, adherence to standardized protocols, and interpretation by radiologists familiar with population-specific disease patterns. When embedded within structured clinical pathways, targeted screening supports early diagnosis, guides multidisciplinary management, and helps prevent avoidable complications in vulnerable pediatric populations.

title: State-of-the-Art Imaging Biomarkers in Screening of Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease.
abstract: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) is the leading global cause of death and evolves over decades through a prolonged subclinical phase, providing a critical opportunity for early detection and prevention. Traditional risk prediction models estimate future cardiovascular risk but may under- or overestimate individual risk, particularly in borderline- and intermediate-risk patients, making them insufficient to guide preventive therapy decisions. Imaging biomarkers complement clinical risk assessment by directly detecting and quantifying subclinical atherosclerosis, enabling more personalized preventive strategies. Coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring with noncontrast electrocardiographic (ECG)-gated CT remains the most established and guideline-endorsed imaging biomarker for risk reclassification. Coronary CT angiography provides incremental prognostic information through assessment of plaque burden, plaque composition, and high-risk plaque features, while emerging techniques, including quantitative plaque analysis and pericoronary adipose assessment, further characterize plaque biology and inflammatory activity. Beyond coronary imaging, extracoronary biomarkers, including carotid and aortic imaging, epicardial adipose tissue, and arterial stiffness assessments provide complementary information about systemic vascular and cardiometabolic health. In addition, opportunistic biomarkers identified at routine CT and MRI examinations, such as incidental coronary and extracoronary calcifications, breast arterial calcification, hepatic steatosis, visceral adiposity, sarcopenia, osteoporosis, and cerebral imaging markers, expand opportunities for cardiovascular risk assessment without additional imaging or radiation. Although many emerging biomarkers require further standardization and outcome-based validation, integration of imaging biomarkers with clinical risk factors, standardized reporting, and artificial intelligence has the potential to improve ASCVD risk stratification and enable more precise and personalized cardiovascular prevention.

title: ARNAI: Artifact Removal Network Based on Autoencoding and Inpainting for Robust Spinal Image Segmentation and Measurement.
abstract: Purpose To develop an artificial intelligence framework, robust to spinal implants, for automated measurement of spinopelvic parameters on postoperative radiographs. Materials and Methods Lateral lumbar spine radiographs from two institutions (internal dataset [ n = 2486]: January 2017-December 2024; external dataset [ n = 217]: October 2021-September 2025) were retrospectively reviewed. The Restore, Segment, and Measure (RSM) framework was developed, incorporating a novel Artifact Removal Network based on Autoencoding and Inpainting (ARNAI) to mitigate implant-related artifacts. Segmentation and spinopelvic parameter (including segmental Cobb angle [SCA]) measurement performance relative to expert reference measurements were assessed using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), mean absolute error (MAE), Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Results With ARNAI added to the segmentation pipeline, the mean DSC increased to 0.870 from 0.814, with marked gains at L3-L5. For implant-containing radiographs in the internal test set, rejected radiographs decreased by 64.21% (95 to 34), and the L4-L5 SCA MAE decreased to 4.7° from 16.2°-15.6° (~ 70% reduction); this remained significant after correction. For the external test set, rejected radiographs decreased by 65.45% (110 to 38), and the L4-L5 SCA MAE decreased to 9.5°-9.7° from 14.2°-14.5° (~ 33% reduction); however, this improvement did not remain significant after correction, and agreement with expert references remained limited. Conclusion The RSM framework improved automated spinopelvic parameter measurement in implant-containing postoperative radiographs, with the greatest benefit observed for L4-L5 SCA estimation in the internal dataset. In the external dataset, error was reduced but agreement remained limited. © RSNA, 2026.

title: Interpretable Deep Learning for Opportunistic Screening of Left Ventricular Dysfunction Screening Using Chest Radiographs.
abstract: Purpose To develop and evaluate a deep learning model (DLLV) for identifying reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) on chest radiographs (CXRs) and assess its potential as a prescreening tool for selective transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) in health checkup populations. Materials and Methods Same-day CXR-TTE pairs obtained between January 2016 and September 2021 were retrospectively collected for model development. Counterfactual learning was applied to enhance model performance and interpretability. External testing included one tertiary referral center cohort and two health checkup cohorts. Discrimination was evaluated using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), and DLLV-based prescreening was evaluated by estimated TTE reduction and missed-case burden. Results The development dataset included 24,674 patients (32,135 CXR-TTE pairs); external cohorts included 5440, 28,034, and 6085 patients (53-62% male). DLLV achieved an AUC of 0.86 (95% CI: 0.84, 0.88) for LVEF ≤ 40% in the tertiary referral cohort. In health checkup cohorts, AUCs were 0.92-0.97 for LVEF ≤ 40%, with AUPRCs of 0.04 in both cohorts, corresponding to 87-fold (95% CI: 16, 404) and 37-fold (95% CI: 3, 251) enrichment over baseline prevalence. Counterfactual reinforcement learning produced heatmaps with greater heart localization precision ( P < .001 for all) and higher AUC for LVEF < 50% ( P = .04). DLLV-based prescreening estimated TTE volume reductions up to 85% while identifying all 12 and 7 individuals with LVEF ≤ 40%. Conclusion DLLV identified reduced LVEF on CXRs across external test cohorts and showed potential as a prescreening tool for selective TTE in health checkup populations. ©RSNA, 2026.

title: Agentic Automation of BT-RADS Scoring Using an End-to-End System for Standardized Glioma Follow-up Assessment.
abstract: The Brain Tumor Reporting and Data System (BT-RADS) standardizes posttreatment MRI response assessment in patients with diffuse gliomas but requires complex integration of imaging trends, medication effects, and radiation timing. An end-to-end multiagent large language model and convolutional neural network system for automated BTRADS classification was developed and evaluated. Five hundred nine consecutive posttreatment glioma MRI examinations (March 2017-July 2021) from a single center were retrospectively evaluated. An extractor agent identified clinical variables from notes using gpt-oss (OpenAI, 20-billion parameters). A scorer agent applied BTRADS decision logic integrating these with quantitative volumetrics. System accuracy was compared against initial assessments, using expert annotation as the reference standard. Four hundred ninety-two examinations were evaluable. Overall system accuracy was 76.0% (374/492) versus 57.5% (283/492) for initial assessments, an absolute difference of +18.5 percentage points ( P < .001). Cohen kappa between the system and the reference standard was 0.71. The system achieved high sensitivity in context-dependent categories (BT-1b; 100%; BT-1a, 92.7%; BT-3a, 87.5%) and moderate sensitivity for threshold-dependent categories (BT-3c, 74.8%; BT-2, 69.2%; BT-4, 69.3%; BT-3b, 57.1%). The BT-4 positive predictive value was 92.9%. These results support further evaluation of this system as a clinical decision-support tool, with local open-weight inference preserving data privacy.

title: Comparative Performance of Federated and Centralized Learning for Brain Tumor Classification and Segmentation.
abstract: Purpose To compare federated learning (FL) and centralized learning (CL) performance for brain tumor classification and segmentation and examine whether specific configurations confer measurable performance advantages. Materials and Methods In this systematic review and meta-analysis, Medline, EMBASE, PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched from inception to March 4, 2026. Classification accuracy was pooled using random-effects meta-analysis, with heterogeneity quantified using I 2 ; other metrics were summarized descriptively. Paired differences in classification accuracy and Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) were assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Mixed-effects meta-regression and subgroup analyses evaluated whether specific configurations were associated with performance differences. Results Of 3,880 records identified, 50 studies were included (26 classification/detection, 26 segmentation; 2 in both). Within-study differences between FL and CL performance were -0.87 percentage points (pp) for classification accuracy (95% CI [-3.32, +1.44]; P = .41, k = 13) and -1.29 pp for segmentation DSC (95% CI [-4.23, +0.81]; Holm-corrected P = .50, k = 11). In unmatched single-arm analyses, pooled classification accuracy was 96.77% for FL (k = 18) versus 96.86% for CL (k = 9); the pooled DSC for segmentation was 84.95% (k = 24) versus 84.61% (k = 11). Heterogeneity was high (I 2 =93.3-96.5%); the 95% prediction interval for FL accuracy was 86.72-100%. Aggregation strategy, training sample size, task category, and independent and identically distributed (IID) versus non-IID partitioning were not associated with performance differences (all P ≥ .38). Conclusion There was no evidence of paired differences between FL and CL in brain tumor classification accuracy or segmentation DSC, and no specific configuration conferred a measurable performance advantage. © RSNA, 2026.

title: Multimodal Transformer Integrating CT and Pathology for Postoperative Risk Stratification in Stage I Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: Purpose To develop and evaluate an interpretable, multimodal deep learning model to improve postoperative risk stratification and predict adjuvant therapy benefit in stage I non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Materials and Methods In this multicenter retrospective study of patients with stage I NSCLC, a multimodal model called the Deep Learning-Radiomic-Text Transformer (DLRTransformer) was developed by integrating multiview 2.5-dimensional deep learning features from CT scans, radiomics, clinical variables, and prognostic embeddings extracted from pathology reports using a large language model. A central transformer architecture fuses these features to predict disease-free survival. Model performance was evaluated on independent external datasets and compared with guideline-based risk stratification. Associations between model-derived risk scores and tumor microenvironment features were analyzed to assess biologic interpretability. Results A total of 1073 patients (mean age ± SD, 60.8 years ± 9.8; 550 male) were enrolled from five centers. On external datasets, DLRTransformer demonstrated robust prognostic performance (concordance index, 0.77-0.78), outperforming the guideline-based risk stratification (concordance index, 0.60-0.65). Risk scores were associated with tumor microenvironment phenotypes, including increased neoplastic cellularity and reduced tertiary lymphoid structures. A treatment-by-risk interaction was observed (interaction hazard ratio [HR], 0.14; 95% CI: 0.06, 0.32; P < .01). In propensity score-matched subcohorts, adjuvant therapy improved disease-free survival in high-risk patients (HR, 0.30; 95% CI: 0.11, 0.84; P = .02) but not in low-risk patients (HR, 1.70; 95% CI: 0.97, 2.99; P = .06). Conclusion The DLRTransformer improved postoperative risk stratification compared with guideline-based risk stratification and identified patients with stage I NSCLC who benefited from adjuvant therapy.

title: Screening Digital Breast Tomosynthesis Performance across Age Groups: Analysis of 302 700 Examinations.
abstract: Purpose To compare screening digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) performance metrics across age groups. Materials and Methods In this retrospective study, screening mammograms acquired from January 1, 2013, to June 30, 2019, at an academic medical center were reviewed. Each examination included combined digital two-dimensional mammography and DBT and was categorized as true positive, false positive, true negative, or false negative based on 1-year follow-up. Performance metrics were calculated according to Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System definitions and compared across age groups using multivariable generalized estimating equation models. Results Among 93 617 female individuals (mean age, 58 years ± 12 [SD]) who underwent 302 700 DBT examinations, cancer detection rate (CDR) increased with age, from 2.9 per 1000 examinations (208 of 70 549) at ages 40-49 years to 8.3 per 1000 (399 of 48 205) at ages 70-79 years and 10.6 per 1000 (127 of 12 018) at age 80 years and older. Sensitivity increased from 72.5% among those aged 40-49 years to 91.7% among those aged 70-79 years (P < .001). The abnormal interpretation rate (AIR) was highest among those aged 40-49 years (9.3%) and lowest among those aged 80 years and older (5.5%), with corresponding specificities of 91.0% and 95.5% (all P < .001). Positive predictive value (PPV1) increased with age, from 3.2% among those aged 40-49 years to 19.2% among those aged 80 years and older (P < .001). Conclusion Screening DBT performance improved with advancing age, demonstrating higher CDRs, sensitivity, specificity, and PPV1, along with lower AIRs. Keywords: Age, Breast Cancer, Digital Breast Tomosynthesis, Mammography, Screening, Breast See also the commentary by Hussain in this issue. title: Risk-adapted MRI Protocols for the Detection of Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer.
abstract: Purpose To compare the diagnostic performance and clinical utility of three MRI protocols for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) according to prebiopsy risk. Materials and Methods This retrospective study included 390 male patients who underwent prostate multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) between January 2019 and April 2024 for suspected csPCa, followed by biopsy. Patients were stratified by Rotterdam Prostate Cancer Risk Calculator score into low-risk (<4%), intermediate-risk (4%-9%), and high-risk (≥10%) groups. Three datasets were generated from each examination: mpMRI (T2-weighted imaging, diffusion-weighted imaging [DWI], and dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging), unenhanced MRI (multiplanar T2-weighted imaging and DWI), and short MRI (axial T2-weighted imaging and DWI). Overall, 1170 datasets were randomly assigned to 10 expert radiologists (117 examinations each). Diagnostic performance for grade group 2 or greater cancer and clinical utility metrics were compared across risk groups. Results Among the 390 patients (median age, 66 years [IQR, 61-71 years]), csPCa prevalence was 34.4% (134 of 390). In low-risk patients, short MRI demonstrated the highest sensitivity (95% [21 of 22]), with no significant differences among protocols (all P ≥ .21) and greatest potential for safe biopsy avoidance (84 biopsies avoided per missed csPCa). In intermediate-risk patients, mpMRI showed higher sensitivity (83% vs 72% for unenhanced MRI and 62% for short MRI; P = .012 for mpMRI vs short MRI) and higher biopsy efficiency (1.11 vs 0.85 for mpMRI vs unenhanced MRI). In high-risk patients, protocol-related differences were minimal (all P ≥ .12). Conclusion mpMRI was associated with improved sensitivity and biopsy efficiency in intermediate-risk patients, whereas protocol differences were limited in low- and high-risk groups; these findings support risk-adapted selection of MRI protocols. Keywords: MR-Dynamic Contrast-enhanced, MR Imaging, Urinary, Prostate, Neoplasms-Primary, Efficacy Studies, Prostatic Neoplasms, MRI, Contrast Medium, Biopsy, Risk Assessment Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA, 2026.

title: Cardiac MRI Strain for Prediction of PET-defined Myocardial Inflammation in Patients with Cardiac Sarcoidosis.
abstract: Purpose To determine whether cardiac MRI strain parameters independently predict PET/CT-defined myocardial inflammation in patients with cardiac sarcoidosis (CS). Materials and Methods This retrospective study included patients with definite or probable CS who underwent cardiac MRI and fluorine 18 fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/CT between January 2010 and October 2022 within 90 days per the Japanese Circulation Society criteria. Strain parameters, including the peak circumferential strain (PCS), peak longitudinal strain (PLS), and diastolic strain rates, were calculated using feature tracking on cine steady-state free precession images. Inflammation was defined by focal FDG uptake using the 17-segment American Heart Association model. T2-weighted and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) images were qualitatively assessed. Segment-level comparisons were performed between inflamed and noninflamed segments. Multivariable logistic regression clustered at the patient level was adjusted for LGE, T2 signal abnormality, age, sex, and left ventricular end-diastolic volume index. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to evaluate the added value of strain metrics over the left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) for inflammation. Results Among 125 included patients (mean age, 59.5 years ± 12.7 [SD]), 60% ( n = 75) had at least one segment with inflammation on FDG PET/CT images. Of these 75 patients, 61% ( n = 46) were male. Segment-level analysis revealed inflammation in 18.1% (385 of 2125) of the segments. The PCS and PLS were lower in inflamed segments than in noninflamed segments (-14.1% vs -18.4% and -10.3% vs -13.0%, respectively; P < .001 for both) and independently predicted inflammation in multivariable analysis (odds ratio, 1.79 and 1.62, respectively; P < .01 for both). Adding PCS to LVEF improved inflammation detection (area under the ROC curve, 0.72 vs 0.63; P = .04). Conclusion Circumferential and longitudinal strain from cardiac MRI independently predicted PET-defined myocardial inflammation. Keywords: MRI, PET/CT, Heart, Cardiomyopathy, Cardiac Strain, Cardiac Sarcoidosis, Myocardial Inflammation © RSNA, 2026.

title: Heart rate fragmentation and variability from real-time cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging using TREND-CMR software.
abstract: Real-time cardiovascular magnetic resonance (rtCMR) is advantageous for imaging irregular cardiac cycles. However, software interpretation of the varied cardiac cycles imaged has been lacking. We developed TREND-CMR software to assess temporal variability in rtCMR. The temporal parameters were extracted from rtCMR scans using principal component analysis and corroborated by corresponding results from ECG and segmentation of the left ventricular blood pool. TREND-CMR provides multiple plots of temporal characteristics and video excerpts of the aberrant heartbeats of a subject. We adapted heart rate fragmentation (HRF), an innovation in electrophysiology, to rtCMR. We also describe new HRF metrics called jerkiness and fragmentation of left ventricular filling time. Applied to the rtCMR scans of 20 volunteers (mainly short axis, but also two-chamber views), jerkiness and HRF inflections suggested differences of two subjects with heart conditions. Regular alteration of beats at inspiration were noted in a subject with respiratory sinus arrhythmia apparent. TREND-CMR also supports motion correction of rtCMR imaging by sorting by respiratory phase. The simple interface, multi-panel plots, video excerpts of atypical beats, will make it easy for the community to quantify HRF and inspect aberrant cycles among a series of imaged beats.

title: Serratia Causing Liver Abscess in a Young Immunocompetent Female: A Rare Case With Literature Review.
abstract: Pyogenic liver abscess (PLA) is a life-threatening condition predominantly caused by enteric Gram-negative bacilli in patients with diabetes, hepatobiliary disease, or immunosuppression. Serratia marcescens is a well-known opportunistic pathogen, typically causing nosocomial infections in compromised hosts. Community-acquired PLA due to S. marcescens in healthy individuals is exceedingly rare. A 28-year-old immunocompetent postpartum female presented with a 40-day history of low-grade fever following a cesarean section, accompanied by fatigue, lower abdominal discomfort, and recent right upper quadrant pain. Initial laboratory investigations revealed marked leukocytosis, microcytic anemia, thrombocytosis, and elevated C-reactive protein (318.76 mg/L). Abdominal computed tomography (CT) demonstrated an 8.5 × 5.8 cm multiloculated hypodense hepatic abscess in segment IV. CT-guided needle aspiration yielded purulent material; pus cultures selectively grew S. marcescens. Concurrently, extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli and Enterococcus faecalis were isolated from urine, while Staphylococcus haemolyticus grew in a single blood culture bottle. Target antimicrobial therapy was adjusted to intravenous meropenem, leading to rapid clinical and inflammatory marker improvement. Because the patient demonstrated prompt clinical stabilization following diagnostic aspiration, percutaneous catheter placement was deferred by a multidisciplinary team. She completed a course of IV meropenem followed by 4 weeks of oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Follow-up ultrasound at 1 month confirmed clinical resolution and regression of the abscess cavity to 1.0 cm. S. marcescens should be considered in the differential diagnosis of PLA, even in immunocompetent individuals presenting with prolonged fever of unknown origin. Early cross-sectional imaging, microbiological aspiration, and multidisciplinary care are essential for prompt resolution without invasive surgical drainage.

title: Delayed Histiocytic Foreign Body Reaction and Granuloma Formation Following Argiform Injection for Soft Tissue Augmentation Mimicking a Lipomatous Tumor on Histopathology: A Case Report.
abstract: As cosmetic procedures gain popularity, the use of nonapproved soft-tissue fillers by unlicensed or untrained practitioners in nonmedical settings is rising. We report a rare case of a histiocytic reaction to foreign material following Argiform injection. A 31-year-old female presented with a 2 year history of an itchy and painful rash on both buttocks. The rash was initially confined to the right buttock but extended to the left several months later; it remained refractory to topical ointments. A skin punch biopsy revealed extensive adipocytic-like cells within the dermis, some of which mimicked lipoblasts. Immunohistochemistry showed the lesional cells were positive for CD68 and negative for S100 and pancytokeratin. A final diagnosis of a histiocytic reaction to foreign material was made. Following the biopsy results, the patient disclosed a history of cosmetic Argiform injections at a spa 4-5 years prior to presentation. This case demonstrates that delayed tissue reactions to Argiform can mimic lipomatous tumors, creating a significant diagnostic pitfall. Clinicopathologic correlation, including a thorough remote medical history, is critical for achieving an accurate diagnosis.

title: Benign Proliferative Nodules in a Giant Congenital Melanocytic Nevus: Diagnostic Challenge and Management.
abstract: Congenital melanocytic nevi are cutaneous malformations present at birth, resulting from a benign proliferation of melanocytes. Although generally benign, they can have significant psychological impacts and carry a non-negligible risk of progression to malignant melanoma. We report a case of a giant congenital melanocytic nevus associated with a perianal mass in an infant, two and half-month-old infant, with no notable medical history, born at term. He was referred for a pigmented perianal swelling located on a large hyperpigmented plaque covering the lower back, buttocks, perineum, external genitalia, and the upper third of the thighs, consistent with a giant nevus. Multiple pigmented maculopapular satellite lesions were present, extending from the scalp to the soles of the feet. All lesions had been present since birth. The general examination was unremarkable. Doppler ultrasound revealed a well-defined, homogeneous, hypoechoic subcutaneous lesion with low vascularity, and skin biopsy confirmed a benign proliferative nodule. The proposed management included surgical excision, neurological and growth development follow-up, and psychosocial support for the infant and the parents. Six months after surgery, follow-up showed no evidence of recurrence, with the infant demonstrating normal neurological function and appropriate growth and developmental progress. This case highlights the importance of an accurate clinical and histological diagnosis and a multidisciplinary approach to management. It contributes to the limited local data from Madagascar and may contribute to the understanding of potential complications and their management.

title: Gastritis Cystica Profunda With High-Grade Dysplasia Mimicking Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor: A Histopathological Pitfall in the Assessment of Submucosal Invasion.
abstract: Background Gastritis cystica profunda (GCP) is an uncommon gastric lesion characterized by displacement of cystically dilated glands into the submucosa. It may present as a submucosal mass mimicking gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST). The coexistence of GCP with high-grade dysplasia is extremely uncommon and may pose a significant diagnostic challenge by simulating invasive carcinoma. Case presentation We report a case of a 54-year-old patient whose endoscopic and radiographic features suggested a GIST in the gastric cardia. Surgical resection was performed. Histopathological examination revealed cystically dilated glands extending into the submucosa, lined by high-grade dysplastic epithelium. Importantly, the muscularis mucosae was focally disrupted, and the submucosal component comprised both dysplastic and nondysplastic glands displaced together within smooth muscle bundles derived from the muscularis mucosae and accompanied by lamina propria-type stroma, supporting mucosal prolapse rather than true invasion. A final diagnosis of high-grade dysplasia arising in GCP was established. Conclusion This case highlights an important diagnostic pitfall in distinguishing pseudoinvasion from true invasive carcinoma in submucosal gastric lesions. Recognition of this entity and careful assessment of the muscularis mucosae together with the character of the displaced glands are essential to avoid overstaging and unnecessary aggressive management.

Background

Gastritis cystica profunda (GCP) is an uncommon gastric lesion characterized by displacement of cystically dilated glands into the submucosa. It may present as a submucosal mass mimicking gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST). The coexistence of GCP with high-grade dysplasia is extremely uncommon and may pose a significant diagnostic challenge by simulating invasive carcinoma.

Case presentation

We report a case of a 54-year-old patient whose endoscopic and radiographic features suggested a GIST in the gastric cardia. Surgical resection was performed. Histopathological examination revealed cystically dilated glands extending into the submucosa, lined by high-grade dysplastic epithelium. Importantly, the muscularis mucosae was focally disrupted, and the submucosal component comprised both dysplastic and nondysplastic glands displaced together within smooth muscle bundles derived from the muscularis mucosae and accompanied by lamina propria-type stroma, supporting mucosal prolapse rather than true invasion. A final diagnosis of high-grade dysplasia arising in GCP was established.

Conclusion

This case highlights an important diagnostic pitfall in distinguishing pseudoinvasion from true invasive carcinoma in submucosal gastric lesions. Recognition of this entity and careful assessment of the muscularis mucosae together with the character of the displaced glands are essential to avoid overstaging and unnecessary aggressive management.

title: Atypical Extramedullary Acute Myeloid Leukemia in Infancy: Bilateral Testicular Swelling and Scalp Lesions at Diagnosis.
abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is rare in infancy, with monocytic subtypes such as acute myelomonocytic leukemia often demonstrating extramedullary involvement. This report describes a 10-month-old male infant presenting with firm bilateral testicular enlargement and multiple parietal scalp nodules, accompanied by leukocytosis and circulating blasts in peripheral blood. Bone marrow examination confirmed French-American-British (FAB) M4 AML. Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated heterogeneous masses, and computed tomography identified scalp chloromas without bone erosion. The patient received AML chemotherapy, resulting in resolution of extramedullary lesions and achievement of remission. This case underscores the importance of early hematologic evaluation in infants with bilateral testicular masses to prevent misdiagnosis. It illustrates the rare occurrence of concurrent testicular and scalp chloromas as the initial manifestation of infant AML.

title: Transient ST-T Changes During Submaximal Exercise Revealing Anomalous Right Coronary Artery Origin in an Asymptomatic Athlete.
abstract: Anomalous aortic origin of a coronary artery is a recognised structural cause of sudden cardiac death in athletes younger than 35 years. Most affected individuals are asymptomatic prior to cardiac events, and resting and exercise electrocardiography (ECG) findings are frequently normal or non-specific, limiting the effectiveness of preparticipation screening. We report a case of a 22-year-old asymptomatic athlete in whom preparticipation screening revealed transient ST-segment depression and T-wave inversions during submaximal exercise and recovery, whereas findings at peak exercise remained normal. Point-of-care echocardiography performed by a sports medicine specialist raised suspicion of an anomalous origin of the right coronary artery from the left aortic sinus of Valsalva, which was subsequently confirmed by computed tomography coronary angiography. High-risk anatomical features included an acute ostial angle and an interarterial course of the right coronary artery. Functional testing with exercise myocardial stress scintigraphy showed no inducible perfusion defect. Following multidisciplinary consultation, a conservative management strategy with activity modification and close follow-up was adopted. This case highlights the potential clinical significance of transient ST-T abnormalities occurring during submaximal exercise and recovery, even in the absence of symptoms or abnormalities at peak workload. In this patient, recognition of this reproducible but non-specific ECG pattern prompted further structural evaluation leading to the diagnosis of AAOCA. It also underscores the limitations of current guidelines in managing asymptomatic athletes with high-risk coronary anatomy but without evidence of inducible ischaemia, supporting the need for individualised decision-making.

title: Infected Complex Odontoma Associated With a Dentigerous Cyst Presenting as a Cutaneous Fistula in the Mandibular Angle: Surgical Management Using Piezoelectric Surgery.
abstract: Odontomas are the most common benign odontogenic hamartomatous tumors. Although typically asymptomatic, they can occasionally lead to severe infectious complications. This report describes a rare case of an infected complex odontoma manifesting as a cutaneous fistula, emphasizing the surgical challenges associated with its anatomical location. A 22-year-old male presented with a 1-month history of a cutaneous fistula at the left mandibular angle and intraoral bone exposure. Radiographic evaluation (panoramic and CBCT) revealed a voluminous radiopaque mass at the mandibular angle, which had severely displaced the third molar toward the inferior border of the mandible. The proximity to the inferior alveolar nerve and the thinness of the remaining bone posed a significant risk of iatrogenic fracture. The patient underwent surgical enucleation of the lesion and extraction of the displaced molar. To mitigate the risk of mandibular fracture and nerve injury, piezoelectric surgery was utilized. The use of ultrasonic inserts allowed for a precise, selective osteotomy and a safe extraction, preserving the structural integrity of the weakened mandible. Histopathological analysis confirmed the diagnosis of a complex odontoma associated with dentigerous cyst. At the 6-month follow-up, the cutaneous fistula had completely resolved with excellent healing and no sign of recurrence. This case highlights that for large, infected odontogenic lesions, the synergy between 3D imaging and minimally invasive technologies like piezosurgery is essential to achieve successful clinical outcomes while minimizing surgical morbidity.

title: Maxillary Expansion With C-Expander Using Digital Planning and CBCT-Based Surgical Guidance: A Case Report.
abstract: This clinical case report describes the clinical management of a patient with a transverse maxillary deficiency treated with a C-expander. The objective is to present the diagnosis, tomographic planning, implantation, and postexpansion evolution. The patient presented with typical characteristics of a transverse maxillary deficiency, with a maxillomandibular discrepancy of 6.8 mm; the insertion of miniscrews was planned using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) and intraoral scanning with BlueSky Plan 4 software. A surgical guide was fabricated, and the C-expander was installed; activation was performed progressively under weekly clinical monitoring. Another CBCT scan was performed after the expansion. Follow-up CT showed transverse improvement with a nearly parallel opening pattern of the median palatine suture of approximately 6.5 mm on the axial view. Dentoalveolarly, the upper intermolar distance increased by 7.1 mm and the lower by 1 mm. Intermolar angulation increased by 2° in the upper arch and 5° in the lower arch; overjet increased by 1 mm and overbite decreased by 15%. Furthermore, the 3D frontal facial reconstruction revealed an increase in the intercanthal distance of 0.3 mm, an increase in the nasal interalar distance of 3.5 mm, and an increase in the nasal base width of 4.4 mm. In conclusion, maxillary expansion using a digitally guided C-expander successfully achieved separation of the midpalatal suture in this patient, with limited dental and facial effects during the immediate postexpansion.

title: A Case Report of a Complete Removable Denture Designed to Restore Function in a Patient With Severe Resorption of the Mandibular Alveolar Ridge Using the Neutral Zone and Flange Techniques.
abstract: Edentulous patients with severe mandibular alveolar ridge resorption struggle with denture stability, which often reduces their quality of life due to mucosal pain and food debris retention. When the inferior alveolar canal is extremely close to the alveolar crest, conventional dentures risk causing severe pain and sensory abnormalities by compressing the inferior alveolar nerve. Thus, conventional fabrication methods face clinical limitations. To stabilize a mandibular complete denture in such cases, it is highly effective to record the dynamics of the denture space and fabricate a prosthesis that harmonizes with these perioral muscle movements. A 77-year-old woman presented with frequent stomatitis caused by ill-fitting dentures and severe masticatory dysfunction. Intraoral and radiographic examinations revealed marked resorption of the mandibular alveolar ridge, placing the inferior alveolar canal in extreme proximity to the alveolar crest. The treatment plan involved fabricating a new maxillary partial denture that strictly balanced the support of the remaining teeth. For the mandible, a complete denture was fabricated using the neutral zone and flange techniques to harmonize with surrounding soft tissue movements. This approach enabled functional contouring by leveraging the dynamic pressure of the perioral muscles. Consequently, denture retention and stability improved dramatically, and denture displacement during speech was successfully suppressed. An evaluation of masticatory function confirmed objective functional recovery. This case demonstrates that for patients with severe alveolar ridge resorption and diminished anatomical supporting tissues, determining the functional form of the denture by accounting for soft-tissue dynamics is highly effective in restoring stability and masticatory function.

title: Mandibular Cemento-Osseous Dysplasia: A Report of Three Cases in Indian Women With Emphasis on Diagnostic Challenges.
abstract: Cemento-osseous dysplasia (COD) is a benign fibro-osseous lesion of the jaw bones that usually affects females and is often seen incidentally on radiographic examination. Its varied clinical and radiographic presentation resembles odontogenic cysts and other fibro-osseous lesions, making diagnosis challenging. This paper highlights three cases of cemento-osseous dysplasia, each with distinct clinical manifestations. These cases demonstrate the varied presentations of cemento-osseous dysplasia, underscoring the need for combined clinical, radiological, and histopathological evaluation for accurate diagnosis.

title: Digital Surgical Management of Traumatic Occlusal Disorder: A Case Report.
abstract: Background Traumatic occlusal disorders secondary to complex mandibular fractures, particularly those involving the condylar region, present a dual challenge: achieving anatomical reduction while restoring physiological function. Conventional surgical approaches are constrained by limited access, soft tissue swelling, and the inherent difficulty of occlusal reconstruction. Case presentation A 33-year-old male presented with an anterior open bite 3 days after maxillofacial trauma. Clinical examination revealed limited mouth opening with preserved facial symmetry. Computed tomography confirmed a sagittal fracture of the right mandibular premolar region and a displaced left condylar neck fracture. A comprehensive digital surgical workflow was deployed, integrating virtual surgical planning, 3D-printed occlusal splint fabrication, and intraoperative guided fracture fixation. Postoperative outcomes demonstrated stable occlusal contact, anatomical condylar reduction, and satisfactory functional recovery. Conclusion The integration of digital surgical techniques enables precise, function-oriented reconstruction in complex mandibular fractures. This approach aligns with the concept of "physiological reduction" and provides a reproducible strategy for managing traumatic occlusal disorders.

title: Recurrent Intermittent Small Bowel Obstruction as an Initial Manifestation of Primary Intestinal Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma: A Case Report and Systematic Literature Review.
abstract: Primary intestinal diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is a rare gastrointestinal malignancy and an uncommon cause of small bowel obstruction (SBO). We report a 70-year-old man with no history of abdominal surgery who presented with recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, vomiting, and transiently resolving SBO. Serial computed tomography (CT) demonstrated a persistent transition point associated with an increasingly evident mesenteric soft tissue mass, initially suspected to represent a neuroendocrine tumor. After repeated presentations and temporary improvement with conservative management, exploratory laparotomy revealed a distal ileal tumor with central mesenteric involvement encasing major mesenteric vessels. Segmental small bowel resection with primary anastomosis was performed, although macroscopic mesenteric disease remained. Histopathological examination confirmed CD10-positive DLBCL, and systemic treatment with six cycles of R-CHOP was initiated. A structured search of MEDLINE and Embase identified 78 publications describing 87 adult cases of intestinal lymphoma presenting with SBO. DLBCL was the most frequently reported subtype, and the ileum was the most commonly specified anatomical location. However, recurrent obstruction with transient clinical and radiological improvement was rarely emphasized. This case demonstrates that temporary resolution of obstructive symptoms does not exclude a persistent pathological lead point. Recurrent SBO in a patient without previous abdominal surgery, particularly when serial imaging demonstrates evolving mesenteric or intestinal abnormalities, should prompt renewed investigation for an underlying malignancy, including intestinal lymphoma. Repeat cross-sectional imaging, multidisciplinary reassessment, and individualized consideration of operative exploration may facilitate timely diagnosis while avoiding conclusions that transient improvement represents definitive resolution.

title: Accurate Localization of the Internal Opening in a Cryptoglandular Anal Fistula: Complementary Roles of Goodsall's Rule, MRI, and Intraoperative Assessment: A Case Report.
abstract: Accurate localization of the internal opening is essential for successful surgical management of cryptoglandular anal fistulas. Although Goodsall's rule remains a useful clinical guide, accurate delineation of fistula anatomy often requires complementary assessment with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and intraoperative evaluation. We report the case of a 34-year-old healthy man presenting with a recurrent perianal fistula characterized by intermittent swelling and purulent discharge. The external opening was located at the 2 o'clock position, more than 3 cm from the anal verge. Preoperative MRI demonstrated a curved transsphincteric fistulous tract extending to an internal opening at the posterior midline without secondary extensions or abscess. The internal opening was confirmed intraoperatively by clinical assessment and hydrogen peroxide injection through the external opening. The extrasphincteric portion of the tract and surrounding chronically inflamed tissue were excised (partial fistulectomy), whereas the transsphincteric portion crossing the external anal sphincter was treated by lay-open fistulotomy to minimize additional sphincter tissue sacrifice. The postoperative course was uneventful, with complete wound healing within 2 months and no impairment of continence. This case illustrates that accurate localization of the internal opening is best achieved through the complementary use of clinical assessment, Goodsall's rule, MRI, and intraoperative confirmation, thereby facilitating appropriate surgical planning and sphincter-preserving treatment.

title: CNS Neoscytalidium dimidiatum : A Rare Cause of Fungal Brain Abscess.
abstract: Neoscytalidium dimidiatum is a dematiaceous fungus that primarily affects plants but can rarely act as an opportunistic pathogen in humans, particularly in immunocompromised patients. It typically causes superficial skin and nail infections in tropical regions; however, central nervous system (CNS) infections are extremely rare. The neurotropism of this fungus is not well understood, but hematogenous spread from cutaneous or pulmonary foci has been hypothesized. A 60-year-old male with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) treated with acalabrutinib, a second-generation Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor, presented with a 3-day history of personality changes, tension-type headache, and progressive right-sided weakness accompanied by dizziness. Physical examination revealed right hemiplegia and homonymous hemianopia. Brain MRI demonstrated a left parietal multiloculated ring-enhancing intra-axial lesion measuring 3.5 × 2 × 2.8 cm3, exerting mass effect on the ipsilateral lateral ventricle and causing rightward midline shift, with associated vasogenic edema and diffusion restriction. Given the immunocompromised state and atypical imaging findings, the patient underwent a left parietal stereotactic aspiration of the lesion. Histopathological examination using Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) staining revealed numerous septate, branching hyphae within the brain parenchyma and vessel walls, confirming an angioinvasive fungal infection. Serum beta-D-glucan was markedly elevated at 238 pg/mL, while galactomannan was negative. Fungal culture confirmed Neoscytalidium dimidiatum, identified based on colony morphology, microscopic characteristics, arthroconidia formation, and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry. Dual antifungal therapy was initiated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B and voriconazole, with subsequent dose escalation and route conversion. The patient was followed for ~12 months and survived with residual right-sided motor deficits. The present case underscores the importance of early diagnosis, prompt surgical management, and appropriate antifungal therapy in improving outcomes for patients with CNS Neoscytalidium dimidiatum infection, particularly in the context of hematological malignancy and BTK-inhibitor-associated immunosuppressive therapy.

title: Rapidly Progressive Buschke-Löwenstein Tumor Managed With Wide Local Excision and Healing by Secondary Intention: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: Buschke-Löwenstein tumor (BLT) is a rare, locally aggressive anogenital tumor associated predominantly with low-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 and 11. BLT is classically described as a slow-growing lesion predominantly affecting middle-aged men who are immunocompromised; cases of rapid progression are rarely reported. We present the case of a 23-year-old male with a progressively enlarging perianal mass over 1 year that was accompanied by rectal pain and intermittent bleeding. He reported prior unprotected heterosexual intercourse, though serologic testing for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B/C was negative. CT imaging revealed a fungating lesion entirely distal to the dentate line without evidence of internal extension. Subsequently, the patient underwent wide local excision with electrocautery fulguration, and the wound was managed with healing by secondary intention. Histopathology revealed clear margins around a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) without high-grade dysplasia or carcinoma; in situ hybridization (ISH) confirmed HPV types 6 and 11, without detection of high-risk HPV. A review of the literature on BLT epidemiology, histopathology, differential diagnosis, and management is presented. This case illustrates that BLT can progress rapidly in young, immunocompetent individuals and highlights that healing by secondary intention following wide local excision is a viable option in appropriately selected cases.

title: Right Anterior Sectionectomy for Hepatic Helminthic Infection Mimicking Cholangiocarcinoma: A Case Report.
abstract: We present the case of a patient with an unexpected pathological finding of degenerate roundworm infection on histology for a liver resection for presumed intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Helminthic infection of the liver is uncommon in developed and metropolitan regions and this patient had no risk factors for such. The only potentially risk factor for complications of the infection was the presence of long-term immunosuppression in the setting of Crohn's disease. The imaging, including computer tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan, was suggestive of a malignant process and thus the patient was consented and brought forward for segments five and eight liver resection. Interestingly the frozen section analysis and formal pathology confirmed a helminthic infection. The patient made an unremarkable recovery and remains well to date. Liver helminth infection mimicking malignancy is rare, however should always be considered as a differential diagnosis for atypical liver imaging findings.

title: Catecholamine-Secreting Retroperitoneal Paraganglioma: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: Introduction Paragangliomas are rare neuroendocrine tumors arising from autonomic paraganglia. These tumors have metastatic potential, and histopathological findings alone cannot reliably predict their biological behavior. Clinical manifestations range from the classic triad of headache, diaphoresis, and palpitations to incidental findings in asymptomatic patients. Case presentation A 75-year-old man was incidentally found to have a 5 cm retroperitoneal mass adjacent to the right renal hilum. Biochemical testing confirmed marked catecholamine hypersecretion, and 18F-FDOPA PET/CT demonstrated isolated uptake within the lesion without additional disease. Preoperative preparation included progressive alpha-adrenergic blockade with doxazosin for approximately 1 month, followed by atenolol for heart rate control. An open approach through a right subcostal hemichevron incision was selected because the tumor was located between the right renal artery and vein and lateral to the inferior vena cava. During dissection, an iatrogenic renal artery injury with intraoperative hemorrhage occurred, necessitating en bloc removal of the tumor, right kidney, and right adrenal gland. Histopathological examination confirmed a paraganglioma with a Ki-67 proliferation index below 1%, focal nuclear atypia, no mitotic figures, no tumor necrosis, no vascular invasion, and microscopic margin involvement. Immunohistochemistry was positive for Chromogranin A, synaptophysin, GATA-3, and S100. Germline testing using a 14-gene pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma panel identified no reported pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants. At 6 months, contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominopelvic computed tomography showed no evidence of local recurrence or metastatic disease, and plasma and urinary metanephrines had normalized, consistent with postoperative biochemical remission. The patient remains under joint endocrinology and urology follow-up with lifelong annual clinical and biochemical surveillance. Discussion and conclusion This case highlights the diagnostic and surgical challenges of a functioning perihilar retroperitoneal paraganglioma. Careful endocrine preparation, vascular planning, multidisciplinary management, and lifelong surveillance are essential, particularly when the surgical margin is microscopically involved.

title: Genetic Heterogeneity in Renal Cell Carcinoma: A Case of Concurrent Clear Cell and Papillary Renal Carcinomas.
abstract: Background/objectives Recent advancements in genetic research have significantly enhanced the understanding of renal cell carcinoma (RCC), now recognized as a heterogeneous group with distinct genetic features. This case report is aimed at illustrating its genetic diversity and implications for diagnosis and treatment. Methods A middle-aged man presented with an incidental finding of RCC in the right kidney on computer tomography (CT) performed for a persistent cough. Comprehensive radiological and blood tests were conducted, followed by a total right nephrectomy. Histological examination showed a concurrent appearance of two manifestly different tumors in the kidney. Molecular analyses, including SNP array and next-generation sequencing (NGS), were conducted to identify genetic mutations and assess clonality. Results The nephrectomy identified two distinct tumors: a clear cell RCC (ISUP/WHO grade 3, pT1b) and a papillary RCC (ISUP/WHO grade 2, pT1a). Molecular analysis confirmed VHL , TP53 , and SETD2 mutations in the clear cell RCC, whereas no mutations were detected in the papillary RCC. The SNP array revealed significant chromosomal differences, suggesting the tumors were not clonally related. Follow-up imaging detected an adrenal metastasis from the clear cell RCC. The metastasis showed a VHL and SETD2 mutation, which undoubtedly proved to be derived from the clear cell RCC. Conclusions This case underscores the genetic heterogeneity of RCC and the importance of molecular profiling in guiding diagnosis and treatment. The distinct genetic profiles of the two tumors suggest they are not clonally related, highlighting the complexity of RCC and the need for individualized therapeutic approaches.

title: Cerebral Manifestation of Miliary Tuberculosis Mimicking a Parasitic CNS Infection.
abstract: The neuroradiological findings of central nervous system (CNS) manifestations of miliary tuberculosis can be misinterpreted as parasitic infections due to their low prevalence in the European population. We present the case of a 30-year-old woman in whom CNS tuberculosis was initially misdiagnosed as a parasitic infection due to the absence of pulmonary symptoms. She immigrated to Germany from Madagascar and had lived in Europe for 14 months by the time she presented to our department with an incidental MRI finding suggestive of a manifestation of toxoplasmosis. The T1-weighted axial brain MRI scan revealed multifocal, rim-enhancing lesions that were suggestive of parasitic infection. Following a chest CT scan that revealed miliary tuberculosis, the diagnosis was revised to neurotuberculosis. This was confirmed by a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) that detected the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex in the sputum sample. The patient achieved remission following 12 months of antituberculosis therapy. In conclusion, neurotuberculosis should be considered in the differential diagnosis of infections presenting with multifocal CNS manifestations on neuroimaging scans in European patients, particularly those with a migration background.

title: Induced Membrane Reconstruction of a 6-cm Ulnar Defect With Concurrent Revision Bone Grafting of Radial Nonunion Following Gustilo-Anderson Type IIIB Open Forearm Fracture: A Case Report.
abstract: The induced membrane technique (IMT) is a two-stage reconstructive procedure for critical-sized bone defects. We report a 31-year-old male who sustained a Gustilo-Anderson grade IIIB open fracture of the radius and ulna following a high-energy dirt bike injury, complicated by Serratia marcescens fracture-related infection and septic nonunion. Intraoperative debridement at Stage 1 revealed a 6-cm defect of the ulna, which was managed with an antibiotic-impregnated polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) spacer. A concomitant radial nonunion, identified on postdebridement CT, was addressed at Stage 2 with concurrent revision open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) and autogenous femoral bone grafting. Culture-directed oral antibiotic therapy was administered following Stage 1. Mature bridging callus was noted at 6 months and confirmed at both bones at approximately 22 months postinjury, with infection eradication confirmed at Stage 2. Prior to subsequent elbow procedures, the patient demonstrated a Mayo Elbow Performance Score of 65 (fair), with an elbow arc of motion of 60°-140° and forearm rotation of 70° pronation and 75° supination. This case illustrates the utility of IMT for ulnar reconstruction in the setting of fracture-related infection, and highlights a forearm-specific biomechanical consideration: Fixing the ulna at a set length via the IMT spacer construct while shortening the radius for nonunion compression may alter radioulnar variance, a single-case observation that we hypothesize could have implications for DRUJ and elbow mechanics and warrants further study.

title: Pyogenic Sacroiliitis in Older Adults Presenting With Massive Retroperitoneal Abscess: A Case Report.
abstract: Pyogenic sacroiliitis (PSI) is an uncommon form of septic arthritis and is frequently diagnosed late in older adults because initial symptoms are nonspecific and imaging findings may be misattributed to other sources of infection. We report two older patients with PSI complicated by massive retroperitoneal and gluteal abscesses, highlighting the importance of early recognition and, when indicated, timely surgical source control. Case 1 was an 83-year-old woman in whom a conspicuous retroperitoneal abscess and abnormal urinalysis led to suspicion of an intra-abdominal or urinary tract source, delaying recognition of PSI. Despite antibiotics, she deteriorated with organ dysfunction; re-evaluation of the initial magnetic resonance imaging MRI identified the sacroiliac joint as the primary focus, and staged surgical drainage procedures were required, followed by a prolonged recovery. Case 2 was a 70-year-old woman who presented in septic shock after failing outpatient treatment for presumed lumbar spine disease. Based on the diagnostic pitfalls in Case 1, PSI was immediately suspected; emergency drainage of both retroperitoneal and gluteal collections was performed on the day of presentation, which was followed by rapid stabilization and recovery. These cases emphasize that, in older patients with low back or gluteal pain, the concurrent presence of retroperitoneal and gluteal abscesses should prompt careful evaluation of the sacroiliac joint. These observations suggest that early diagnosis and timely assessment for surgical source control may contribute to favorable outcomes in severe cases.

title: Prenatal Detection of HSPG2 -Related Dyssegmental Dysplasia, Silverman-Handmaker Type: A Rare Case Report.
abstract: Introduction HSPG2 -related dyssegmental dysplasia (heparan sulfate proteoglycan 2) is an extremely rare and severe autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia. The low incidence and the overlapping features with other types of lethal skeletal dysplasia represent the main challenges in diagnosis. Early diagnosis is essential and can be achieved by ultrasound examination and genetic analysis. This report describes a case of HSPG2 -related dyssegmental dysplasia, Silverman-Handmaker type (DDSH) diagnosed prenatally through a combination of detailed ultrasound imaging and subsequent genetic analysis. Case presentation A 21-year-old pregnant lady (G2P1) was referred to our center at 17-week gestation upon the detection of severe shortening of fetal limbs. Detailed ultrasound examination revealed small for gestational age, and specific craniofacial features such as severe micrognathia, short neck, microcephaly, prominent eyes, and occipital encephalocele. Other abnormalities were detected in extremities in the form of bowing of lower limbs, severe tetramicromelia, and upper limbs in a fixed flexion. Amniocentesis for whole exome sequencing was performed. It showed a homozygous pathogenic variant in the HSPG2 gene (c.11565+1G>A), a result consistent with the genetic diagnosis of autosomal recessive HSPG2 -related DDSH. Medical termination was performed based on the decision of parents. Parents signed a written consent for the publication of this case report. Discussion Findings of this report support the growing evidence of the phenotypic spectrum and genetic underpinnings of the lethal disorder of HSPG2 -related DDSH, emphasizing the importance of early and accurate diagnosis for optimal patient care. DDSH can be diagnosed prenatally using fetal ultrasound as early as 13 weeks. Radiographic assessment and molecular analysis of the HSPG2 gene are essential for confirming the prenatal diagnosis. Accurate diagnosis enables appropriate healthcare delivery and facilitates informed reproductive decision-making, including prenatal diagnosis and preimplantation genetic testing in future pregnancies.

title: Ovarian Yolk Sac Tumor in a 10-Year-Old Girl Following Metachronous Bilateral Mature Ovarian Teratomas.
abstract: Background Ovarian germ cell tumors are the most common ovarian malignancies in children. Because these patients have a notable risk of developing metachronous bilateral tumors or recurrences, maximizing the preservation of ovarian tissue during initial surgery is critical to protecting future fertility and endocrine function. Objective A previously healthy 8-year-old girl underwent emergency laparotomy for ovarian torsion, resulting the right oophorectomy, with histopathology confirming a mature teratoma. Sixteen months later, a contralateral ovarian mass was detected and treated with ovarian-sparing excision, also diagnosed as a mature teratoma. At age 10 (10 months after the second excision), she was found to have an 8 cm pelvic tumor and elevated α -fetoprotein. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed complex solid and cystic components suggestive of a malignant germ cell tumor, with no metastases on computed tomography/MRI. The mass was removed intact at exploratory laparotomy, yielding a diagnosis of Fédération Internationale de Gynécologie et d'Obstétrique (FIGO) Stage 1A ovarian yolk sac tumor. She was discharged after completing combination chemotherapy. Currently, she is 16 years old and being managed with hormone replacement therapy. Conclusions The presented case highlights a disadvantage of overzealous oophorectomy. Detorsion of the seemingly necrotic ovary followed by second-look surgery could have preserved some ovarian function.
